stories.headline: Tom Aspinall vacates UFC heavyweight title amid ongoing eye issues
stories.summary: Tom Aspinall has decided to vacate his UFC heavyweight title as a result of "ongoing complications" with injuries to his eyes.
stories.body:
Tom Aspinall has decided to vacate his UFC heavyweight title as a result of "ongoing complications" with injuries to his eyes.

The Brit confirmed his decision via a statement on social media on Monday, saying he was "gutted." Aspinall (15-3) said he had been back sparring and had a new fight date locked in, but an accident in training has brought a further set-back.

Aspinall has not fought since his no contest against Ciryl Gane last October, when he was poked in the eyes. He was forced to retire from the fight in the first round and has since had multiple surgeries in both his eyes.

"Ongoing complications with my eyes mean I cannot get medically cleared to fight right now," Aspinall said.

"I've had multiple surgeries, accidents and infections, and done everything possible to get back to competing.

"I had previously agreed to a fight date and was back sparring, feeling great and ready to compete when an accident caused further damage to my right eye. This means more time away from the sport, and right now, the timing of my return is unclear.

"I've now made the decision to vacate the heavyweight title. I've asked the UFC to allow me to make this statement because I don't want to hold the heavyweight division up. I know what it's like to have your career put on hold and I want the other fighters to have the opportunity to compete for the title."

In June, Aspinall confirmed he was back in full training and working towards a rematch with Gane, who beat Alex Pereira that month.

Following Gane's win over Pereira, Aspinall said on his YouTube channel that the was ready for a rematch with the Frenchman and prepared to fight in Paris.

Aspinall stressed he wanted to return to action as soon as possible but on the advice of doctors, would not be fighting in the foreseeable future. The 33-year-old said he

"We have worked closely with different doctors and specialists to try and make my return happen, but unfortunately, it's simply not possible right now," he said. "I'm absolutely gutted. I've chased this dream since I was 10 years old.

"I'm not done. Stepping away from the title is not stepping away from the sport or the dream. I'll continue doing everything I can to get healthy, get cleared and get back to competing as soon as possible."

stories.headline: NFL Week 1 offense explosion: Bears, Ravens, Bills, Jaguars
stories.summary: Chicago (59), Baltimore (41), Buffalo (36) and Jacksonville (34) were among 10 teams that scored 30-plus points Sunday. What happened, and can it continue?
stories.body:
There are few joys in sports like the first Sunday of the NFL season. After an entire offseason without professional football, we finally get a flood of Week 1 games all at once. NFL RedZone springs to life for the first time since January. Some years, the anticipation can be more exciting than the actual action, with offenses playing in the regular season together for the first time struggling to find a rhythm. This year, though, offensive struggles were few and far between.

Nine different teams scored 30 or more points in the early window on Sunday, just the second time that has ever happened. And with the Vikings unexpectedly making it to 39 points in their comeback win over the Packers, 10 teams scored 30 or more points in all on Sunday. That's the first time that has happened since 2002 and just the third time it has happened on the opening Sunday of the NFL season since the AFL-NFL merger in 1970 (1986 being the other).

Some of those big scores were a product of uncommon circumstances. The Lions and Saints went to overtime, when they each scored a touchdown. The Vikings scored four consecutive touchdowns in the second half to come back against Green Bay, with three of those drives starting deep in Packers territory after a big kickoff return and two defensive turnovers, making life easier for a Carson Wentz-led offense to rack up points. A Bengals defense that forced and recovered four fumbles against the Buccaneers took one to the house for a defensive score and set up the offense with two short fields.

Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show'

Others attempted to keep up in shootouts but fell short. The Texans managed 31 points against a conservative Bills defense in C.J. Stroud's first start since his playoff meltdown. But after driving into the red zone in the last minute of the game, Stroud was sacked twice on the final three plays, including on a three-man rush that produced a game-ending strip sack. And while the Panthers scored 37 points on a day when Bryce Young threw for 361 yards, well, the Bears scored more points on offense than any team has since the Dolphins went for 70 in September 2023.

Today, I'm going to focus on the four other teams that hit 30-plus points and how their offenses got off to blistering-hot starts. The Bears, Bills, Jaguars and Ravens all had high hopes for their offenses heading into Week 1, but they scored a combined 170 points in their season-opening victories. How did they pull that off? Were the defenses more to blame? Or should we be projecting these offenses to lead the league in scoring the rest of the way?

I'll run through all four, starting in Chicago, where the Bears heard Ben Johnson say that he wanted to field the highest-scoring offense in NFL history and proceeded to tie the 2019 Ravens in scoring the most points on offense of any team in NFL history in a season-opening performance.

Jump to:

Bears | Bills | Jaguars | Ravens

Bears 59, Panthers 37
While there will still be concerns about the Bears' defense after it allowed Bryce Young & Co. to score 37 points, defense isn't going to matter if you're approaching 60. In their season opener, the Bears' offense scored more points than they have in any other game in the 105-year history of the franchise. They somehow scored 59 points on offense without a single catch from tight end Colston Loveland, the sort of combination that would seem impossible if it hadn't just played out Sunday afternoon in Charlotte.

To get there, the Bears produced something that we didn't see from them on offense in 2025: big plays on the ground. For all the things the Bears did well during Ben Johnson's first year at the helm, creating big rushes wasn't one of them. They had just four runs of 25 or more yards last season, tied with the Saints for 25th in the NFL.

It took the 2026 Bears all of one game to match their seasonlong total from a year ago. Johnson's offense produced four 25-plus-yard gains on the ground against the Panthers, including touchdown runs of 28 yards (by D'Andre Swift), 29 yards (Caleb Williams) and 61 yards (Kyle Monangai). Swift added a 32-yarder early in the game to make it four. The Bears finished with 291 rushing yards on 39 attempts, averaging 7.5 yards per carry.

The Panthers don't have a great run defense, given that they ranked 24th in DVOA on the ground in 2025. And defensive issues certainly made life easier for the Bears. Carolina inadvertently doubled Rome Odunze over the middle of the field instead of passing him off from one defender to the next as Williams scrambled just before halftime, leaving a free path for the young quarterback to escape a four-man rush and scamper up the sideline for a 29-yard score. The Panthers also didn't get anybody into the A-gap on Swift's 32-yard run in the first quarter, then missed multiple tackle attempts on the newly extended back before he changed fields to pick up extra yardage.

On the whole, though, the Bears were dominant running the ball because they simply overwhelmed the Panthers. Tight end Cole Kmet had one of those games where you can't wait to get back into the building for film review; in addition to making a great catch on a leak concept for a 22-yard touchdown, Kmet made big blocks on Swift and Monangai touchdown runs, driving defenders out of the play to create run lanes. The right side of Chicago's O-line -- highly paid guard Jonah Jackson and budding star Darnell Wright -- had an excellent game. And both Swift and Monangai got more than what was blocked, which wasn't always the case a year ago. The Bears were average on rush yards over expectation per attempt on designed runs last season (NFL Next Gen Stats), but they were comfortably tops in the league in Week 1.

Williams made a number of plays with his legs, but he was also just as spectacular as a passer. The 2024 first overall pick has deservedly lived in the dreams of Bears fans all offseason for the memorable moments he had down the stretch and into the postseason in 2025, creating magic in the fourth quarter for the Bears as they led late comebacks. We know Williams still has that capacity to extend plays and deliver passes that few other quarterbacks on the planet can make, and we saw a little bit of that Sunday.

The touchdown pass to Kmet was inch-perfect. Williams also extended a play, scrambled, then threw against the grain on a deep out to Kalif Raymond for 28 yards. (Raymond surprisingly led the team in targets, catches and receiving yards.) If there had been any need for late-game heroics, Williams was playing like they would have come.

What was really striking, though, was just how in-control Williams looked as a passer, something that wasn't the case on a regular basis last season. The Panthers didn't offer much of a pass rush, as their 16.1% pressure rate was the worst of any team in Week 1, but Williams didn't give them much time to generate one, either. He was really effective early in the game at getting to the end of his drop and getting the ball out quickly. And when Williams did extend plays, they usually produced positive results.

With the ball coming out when it was supposed to within the context of the offense and little pressure from Carolina, Williams was also a more accurate passer. His off-target rate was a league-worst 20.2% a year ago, but it improved to 13.8% in Week 1. That was almost exactly league-average. Williams' minus-6.7% completion percentage over expectation (CPOE) was the worst in football among regular starters in 2025, per NFL Next Gen Stats. His plus-11.4% CPOE on Sunday was the third-best mark of Week 1 and the best mark he has posted in a single game under Johnson.

Are there elements that probably won't stick? Yes. The Bears went 4-for-4 in the red zone and 10-of-14 on third down, rates even the best offenses in football would struggle to hit for any stretch of time. They started three possessions in Carolina territory, turning those drives into 17 points. Plus, the Panthers helped bail the Bears out, including a roughing the passer penalty on second-and-20 and an offside that wiped off a Williams interception at the goal line. The degree of difficulty will increase dramatically over the next two weeks, with the Bears set to face the Vikings and Eagles at home.

While they probably can't count on creating four huge runs every week moving forward, though, there was very little about the Bears' performance that felt fluky or unsustainable. They were an effective team on the ground in 2025, so it's hardly out of the question that they could create more explosive runs this season. Williams looked more comfortable and played more comfortably in his second year under Johnson. If anything, the offense could look even more explosive with Loveland actually figuring into the mix.

They probably won't score 59 points every week, but based on what they did against the Panthers, the Bears absolutely look like they can contend to be the best offense in the NFL this season.

Ravens 41, Colts 23
The Ravens might have also joined the Bears in topping 50 points if they had more healthy wide receivers to play. Zay Flowers racked up 150 receiving yards in the first half before tweaking his hamstring and sitting out the rest of the game. Rookie Ja'Kobi Lane had a touchdown overturned by a penalty before suffering a wrist injury. By the end of the game, LaJohntay Wester and Chris Moore were running routes for Baltimore alongside Rashod Bateman.

By then, of course, the game was already out of reach. If it weren't for a holding penalty on center Jovaughn Gwyn that wiped away that touchdown pass to Lane, the Ravens would have scored touchdowns on each of their first five possessions, gaining 254 yards along the way. And even without two of his top three wide receivers, Lamar Jackson produced a 77-yard touchdown drive and a 43-yard push for a field goal in the fourth quarter, putting any hope of a late Colts comeback to bed.

This was one of the offenses I was most intrigued to watch in Week 1. The Ravens are one of several teams moving a mobile quarterback under center more often this season, a concept I'm going to write about in greater detail later this week. The shift wasn't going to be quite as significant for Jackson, who played in a pro-style offense at Louisville, as it was going to be for the likes of Jayden Daniels and Kyler Murray, but this was still Jackson's first game with new coordinator Declan Doyle after a brilliant three-year stretch under Todd Monken.

The early returns are impressive. Jackson was 6-of-8 for 114 yards operating from under center Sunday, including a 49-yard play to Flowers out of a boot concept to the left, the sort of explosive pass concept the Ravens were hoping to create off play-action by moving Jackson under center more often. One of his two incompletions was a spike to stop the clock, and Bateman was actually open on a scissors concept on the other, only for Jackson to feel pressure around the right side and get the ball out a tick too late. That timing will come more naturally as Jackson's under center more often.

In his first game as his team's primary playcaller, the 30-year-old Doyle delivered on much of the excitement Ravens fans have expressed about the Ben Johnson disciple. He built a great game plan around using Flowers to attack the middle of the field, keeping him away from Indy's top two corners (Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward) in the process. Flowers picked on slot corner Justin Walley, who was no match.

Doyle also got Flowers into the backfield. While that surprisingly included one snap where Flowers lined up at fullback, the more notable play would have been lining him up as a halfback next to Jackson in the second quarter. Flowers came out of the backfield and ran a choice route, which typically requires the receiver to feel the leverage of the coverage and run away into space. The Colts made life easier by simply not covering Flowers at all, and the star wideout took advantage of the missed assignment by taking a short catch 54 yards to the house.

Doyle isn't the first coordinator to get his top wideout into the backfield for a choice route -- the Seahawks, for one, put Jaxon Smith-Njigba in the backfield for his touchdown catch against the Rams in the NFC Championship Game last season -- but it's another wrinkle that creates havoc for opposing defenses. Flowers was on pace for a 300-yard game before his injury. If he can stay on the field, Baltimore's top wideout is going to have a massive season.

One of the other advantages of going under center is creating a more diverse, difficult-to-predict run game and more natural angles for outside zone concepts. Those under-center outside zone runs were Derrick Henry's bread-and-butter in Tennessee, and so it probably shouldn't be any surprise that he excelled in Doyle's debut. Henry ran the ball 24 times for 144 yards and three touchdowns, including a 32-yard touchdown in the second quarter. He had 11- and 22-yard runs on zone concepts during the blowout victory.

Jackson's designed run rate dropped last season, and he had only one designed run Sunday. But the two-time MVP showed that he can still make an impact with his legs. Jackson scored from 5 yards out on a pistol zone-read concept, then added scrambles of 16 and 19 yards, the former seeing Jackson duck under two pass rushers before converting a third-and-16 with his legs. If there were concerns that Jackson had lost an athletic step, it didn't seem to be on the tape in Week 1.

It was promising to see a new-look Ravens offensive line get off to an excellent run-blocking start in Week 1, but the interior is still an obvious weak spot on this offense. Gwyn, debuting at center and making his first career start in his fourth season as a pro, cost the Ravens a touchdown with a holding call. First-round pick Olaivavega Ioane erased a pair of first downs with holding penalties. A blown assignment between Gwyn and left guard John Simpson allowed Grover Stewart to burst through the A-gap unblocked on fourth down in the red zone, quickly blowing up a play that would end with an incompletion and a turnover on downs.

While the Bears are set to face stiffer competition, the Ravens have a soft slate of defenses in the weeks to come. They face the Saints, Cowboys, Titans, Falcons, Browns, Bengals and Bills over the next seven weeks. It's going to be tough to consistently create big plays through the passing game if Flowers is out for any extended period of time, but given that Jackson hit Moore for a 53-yard completion in the second half, there should still be some explosiveness in this offense if Flowers misses a week or two against subpar defensive competition.

Bills 36, Texans 31
This game served as a measure of revenge for Josh Allen, who had appeared to be flummoxed whenever he stepped into Reliant Stadium. The Bills collapsed in the second half in a 22-19 overtime loss to the Texans in the 2019 season, with Allen infamously attempting to hit fullback Patrick DiMarco with a go ball on his first pass attempt in OT. The star quarterback went 9-of-30 with two picks in his return to Houston in 2024, then 16-of-33 for 151 yards with two more interceptions when the Bills lost to the Texans in 2025. There's no shame in struggling against one of the NFL's best defenses, but over the past two years, Allen had posted a 28.2 Total QBR against the Texans and a league-best 72.8 mark against everyone else.

After those three losses in Houston, Allen finally turned things around with his best performance against the Texans on Sunday. It wasn't always pretty, but Allen went 20-of-29 for 334 yards and two touchdowns while adding two more scores as a runner. He also drew a 46-yard pass interference penalty on Kamari Lassiter to set up one of those rushing scores. Lassiter helped get the Bills off the field by tackling Allen short of the sticks on fourth down in the first half, but Allen would have the last laugh.

With 1:41 left in the game and the Bills trailing by one point, Allen took the lead back on a third-and-11 by hitting receiver Joshua Palmer for a 34-yard touchdown past Lassiter. It was a perfect throw in an absolutely critical situation, one in which most quarterbacks would be trying to protect the football and keep their team in position for a field goal to take the lead. It made a huge difference, given that the Texans then had to drive for a touchdown instead of simply needing to get in field goal range, where their drive eventually stalled.

Of course, Lassiter very nearly won the battle and the game for his team. On the snap before the touchdown pass to Palmer, Allen tossed a lob off his back foot in the direction of DJ Moore, who didn't seem to know that the ball was coming. Lassiter turned to make a game-sealing interception, only for the ball to bounce off his chest for an incompletion.

That's an incredibly narrow line to toe as we evaluate Allen's performance and try to draw broader conclusions. If Lassiter catches that, Allen's great game is wasted by a foolish decision late in the contest, and there's still something about playing in that dome that seems to bring the old, dangerous Allen out of the reformed signal-caller. But Lassiter couldn't make the catch, and Allen immediately delivered an incredibly clutch TD pass on the next snap to win the game for the Bills. Likewise, Allen connected with Moore for a 43-yard touchdown on a throw that was nearly tipped away by Reed Blankenship, who might have been a step away from picking it off.

In his first game as head coach, Joe Brady did seem to make one change to the Bills' offense, and it turned out to be an important shift. While Dalton Kincaid was efficient on a per-route basis from 2023 to 2025, the Bills simply didn't use him all that often. Kincaid ran routes on 58% of Buffalo's dropbacks when healthy enough to play, averaging 2.0 yards per route run in the process.

On Sunday, though, Kincaid ran routes on 71% of Allen's dropbacks, trailing only Moore among Bills pass catchers and marking his highest route participation rate since the first half of the 2024 season. Kincaid caught five passes for a career-high 130 yards, including completions of 35, 38 and 40 yards, beating three different Texans defensive backs in the process. Brady used Kincaid as a split-out receiver before motioning him inside to try to create mismatches and conflict with the Texans' defense. This was his best game as a pro.

Kincaid was one of the answers the Bills were hoping to lean on as they dealt with man coverage issues over the past couple of seasons. While teams don't want to play man defense against the Bills out of concerns about Allen's legs, Buffalo's middling receiving corps had left Allen without a receiver who could reliably win against man coverage. From 2024 to 2025, Allen ranked first in the NFL in Total QBR against zone coverage but just 17th against man-to-man defense, a figure that includes his impact as a scrambler.

The Texans surprisingly played into that discrepancy on Sunday. Per Next Gen Stats, Matt Burke's defense played zone on 24 of Allen's 32 dropbacks in Week 1. To be fair, Allen torched both coverages, posting a 130.1 passer rating against zone and a 129.7 mark against man, including the game-winning score to Palmer. The Texans had played man nearly 39% of the time in their 2024 and 2025 victories over Buffalo, with Allen going 6-of-22 for 94 yards and an interception against man coverage across those two games. With a healthy defense, this felt like a changeup gone wrong for DeMeco Ryans.

Could Moore have discouraged the Texans from playing more man? This was a successful debut for the former Panthers and Bears wideout, who caught five passes for 100 yards in addition to drawing that 46-yard pass interference penalty. Most of Moore's success, though, came against zone looks, with Allen hitting him on a pair of in-breakers against Cover 3 and a flood concept before the 43-yard touchdown against Cover 2.

In a game in which the Bills were either ahead or narrowly behind for most of the contest, the Texans also weren't able to pin their star edge rushing duo's ears back and go after Allen. Danielle Hunter knocked away a third-down pass attempt, and Will Anderson Jr. managed a team-high six pressures, but the duo failed to sack Allen once across 32 dropbacks on Sunday. The Texans had two sacks total and managed only three quick pressures after generating seven in both the 2024 and 2025 matchups.

Playing one of the league's best defenses in what hasn't been a very friendly stadium in years past, even an average day from Allen would have been a surprisingly effective performance. But with the Bills' defense allowing the Texans to produce one of their best offensive games of the past year, Brady needed something great from Allen. And while Allen very nearly threw the game away, the second chance the Texans gave the former MVP to win the contest was one too many.

Jaguars 34, Browns 10
I'll finish in Jacksonville, where Trevor Lawrence was facing no such onslaught from the opposing offense. Deshaun Watson ended the first Browns drive with an interception, the second with a dropped interception and the third with a strip sack, while the fourth halted after a fumble by KC Concepcion. While Watson finished 16-of-22 for 205 yards, most of that production came in garbage time. By the time the Browns showed any signs of life on offense in this game, the Jaguars were already up 34-3 and running out the clock.

In his 2026 debut, Lawrence picked up from where he left off in the 2025 regular season, with nearly as many touchdown passes (four) as incompletions (five). He was particularly effective and accurate throwing downfield. On passes traveling 10 or more yards in the air, Lawrence went 10-of-12 for 179 yards and three touchdowns, with one of those incompletions coming on a Brenton Strange drop. That 83.3% completion percentage on intermediate and deep throws would have been the second-best single-game mark for a player with 10 attempts or more in 2025, trailing only Jared Goff's performance against the Rams.

While Lawrence played well and coach Liam Coen mixed in some wrinkles to create throwing lanes off play-action, this frankly looked easy for the Jags on offense. From a Cleveland perspective, too many of these throws were pitch and catch, and when the throws weren't perfect, Jacksonville's receivers made great catches, highlighted by a diving touchdown grab by Parker Washington in the first half. Lawrence had just two tight-window completions all day, which I say not as a knock on his performance but as a reflection of how open Jacksonville's receivers consistently got.

This felt like a Browns defense that sorely missed departed star pass rusher Myles Garrett and defensive coordinator Jim Schwartz. Jared Verse didn't manage a single hurry in his Browns debut, while new defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg had a Browns unit that successfully played a lot of aggressive man coverage under Schwartz instead playing a passive, static zone defense. Lawrence faced zone looks on 20 of his 25 dropbacks and wasn't subject to a single quick pressure all game. The Browns blitzed just three times, even while Lawrence shredded their four-man rush.

Even without Garrett in the mix, limiting Lawrence to one sack (albeit an 11-yard takedown on a third-and-1) was an impressive performance by an offensive line that loomed as a potential weakness heading into the season. Likewise, while the run game wasn't spectacular, the three-headed unit of Bhayshul Tuten, Chris Rodriguez Jr. and Ameer Abdullah managed 121 yards on 25 carries, with a 52% success rate and five runs of 10 yards or more. Jacksonville generated zero rush yards over expected, suggesting that its runners got exactly what was blocked on average throughout the game.

Again, I think that's a testament to how well the Jaguars controlled the line of scrimmage and how little the Browns showed on the defensive side of the ball, where there wasn't enough push. When the Jags did struggle in the run game, it was usually a product of their own mental mistakes, like a pulling blocker overrunning a defender or tripping over a teammate, as opposed to Cleveland forcing the issue.

If the Jaguars had done this against the 2023 or 2025 Browns, this would be a wildly impressive performance. Watching this game back, though, I'm very concerned that the Browns just aren't going to be a good defense or anything resembling the unit we saw with Garrett on the field at his best over the past few seasons. They didn't seem to have any sort of defensive identity and looked like an entirely different unit from the one that kept an awful offense in games a year ago.

Scoring on six of your first seven drives, as the Jags did Sunday, is impressive against any caliber of defense, but this was almost too easy upon further review. Jacksonville's best offensive performance of 2025 was in Week 16, when it scored 34 points on the Broncos and beat the top seed in the AFC on the road. If the Jaguars can do something like that again in Denver when the two teams meet next week, it'll mean a lot more than what we saw against the Browns in Week 1 -- even if it was an impressive performance from Lawrence and his unit in the home opener.

stories.headline: Manchester derby mess shows VAR's quest for perfection is doomed to fail
stories.summary: Erling Haaland's goal in the Manchester derby proved that perfection will always be out of reach for VAR, despite it being there to give us exactly that.
stories.body:
Erling Haaland might just be the perfect goal scorer, but his goal in Manchester City's 1-0 win against Manchester United on Sunday proved that perfection is something that will always be out of reach for VAR (Video Assistant Referee), despite it being there to give us exactly that.

Remember when VAR was introduced into the Premier League in 2019 after a successful trial run at the 2018 FIFA World Cup? It was adopted by the most high-profile league in the world to bring clarity and certainty to the biggest decisions, and put an end to games being decided by the mistakes of officials on the pitch.

No more calamitous offside calls or wrongly issued red cards; no more players getting away with terrible challenges unseen by on-field officials; and, mercifully, no more managers complaining about refereeing mistakes after a defeat.

Controversy would be consigned to history. It was all going to be perfect.

- Manchester derby reaction: City's 10-man master class

- VAR review: Decision behind Manchester derby goal explained

- Staggering numbers behind Premier League's spending power

That has always been the perception of VAR -- the ultimate safety net of a review process that would bring swift on-field justice. But because video technology is in the hands of human operators, perfection is in the eye of the beholder and subjectivity pollutes every decision-making process.

So when you have a scenario such as in the Manchester derby, when Haaland's goal was initially ruled out for offside by assistant referee Stuart Burt, the role of the VAR is to check that the decision is correct. In this case, they had to answer three questions:

1. Was Haaland offside?

2. Was there a foul in the build up to the goal?

3. Were any other players in an offside position?

All of these questions must be answered before the assistant referee's decision is cleared, but because everybody expects perfection, the VAR -- on this occasion Matthew Donohue and his assistant Blake Antrobus -- had to make a subjective decision on No. 2 and No. 3 after semi-automated technology showed that Haaland was actually onside.

There is no foul in the buildup, so question No. 2 is answered quickly, but No. 3 is the one which drags the VAR team into trouble. The officials decide that City's Enzo Fernández is neither challenging for the ball, nor obstructing United defender Lisandro Martínez's path to it, despite the midfielder throwing himself at Josko Gvardiol's cross in an attempt to get his head on it.

And this incident highlights the perennial flaw of VAR. When it comes to a subjective decision, officials will interpret things differently. It can never be a perfect system -- not until AI puts them all out of a job and gets every decision correct in a millisecond.

But here's the irony of it all: In a system that can never be perfect because of the human element, the officials are attempting to make it just that by overthinking and overanalyzing what should be straightforward decisions.

Had Donohue and Antrobus correctly applied the Laws of the Game (Offside is Law 11) they would have quickly asserted that Fernández was attempting to play the ball and was also blocking Martínez's path to it. So he was offside on two counts of the Law. Yet, inexplicably, in their pursuit of making the perfect decision while sitting at the video screen, their attempt to be 100% correct ended with them being 100% wrong.

Perfection was staring the VAR team in the face, written in black-and-white in the Laws of the Game. But they chose to bring their own interpretation and delivered what may go down as the worst VAR mistake the Premier League has ever seen.

Howard Webb, the 2010 World Cup final referee and head of Pro Ref, the new name for the referees' body, said last month that he wanted his VAR officials to meet a high bar for intervention in on-field decisions and only get involved when there was an obvious error by the referee and his assistants. But his instruction does not cater for VAR officials second-guessing themselves and being influenced by concerns over what the reaction will be if they get it wrong. In an attempt to get it right, they miss the obvious, as happened at Old Trafford.

Pro Ref issued a statement three hours after the final whistle on Sunday to admit that Haaland's goal was awarded in "error," but it was too late to change the outcome of the game. Pro Ref got it right in the end, but perfection only arrived when United manager Michael Carrick and his players were back home, nursing a collective sense of injustice.

Haaland's goal could turn out to be significant. United have now equaled their worst start to a Premier League season by taking just four points from four games, so Carrick will start to come under pressure to save his job if the sequence continues. By gaining an additional two points from a game that looked set to head for a draw -- City had been reduced to 10 players on 25 minutes following a red card to Phil Foden -- City's fortuitous victory could be decisive in the title race if they end up winning it by a point or two.

And if Haaland (who is currently on 115) ends his City career with 261 league goals, eclipsing Alan Shearer's Premier League record of 260, will there be an asterisk next to his name because of a goal that should not have counted at Old Trafford?

All of the above are possible outcomes, and anything but perfect. But they would all be a direct consequence of the VAR call during the 199th Manchester derby.

So much for perfection.

All the prop bet recommendations, betting projections and trends are generated by THE BAT X, a system that I've created using advanced methods like those used in MLB front offices, accounting for a variety of factors including player talent, ballparks, bullpens, weather, umpires, defense, catcher pitch-framing and more. stories.headline: NBA offseason recap, early 2026-27 season previews by team
stories.summary: We're looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the regular season by rolling out one team profile each weekday through Sept. 18.
stories.body:
After an eventful July full of big trades, intriguing signings and the game's biggest star shocking everyone by heading East, the NBA offseason is nearly complete. And with the regular-season schedule now out, it's time to start thinking about the 2026-27 season.

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for every team.

Check out the rollout schedule below, with stories added daily:

Quick links:

Free agency buzz | FA grades | Trade grades

Transactions | Schedule | More NBA coverage

Atlantic Division

Philadelphia 76ers: Sept. 14
Key additions: F LeBron James, G Jaylen Brown, G Anfernee Simons, F Dean Wade, G Labaron Philon Jr., G Kentavious Caldwell-Pope

Key subtractions: F Paul George, C Andre Drummond, G Quentin Grimes, G Kelly Oubre Jr.

No team changed its fortunes from April to July as drastically as the 76ers. Taking advantage of Boston's desire to get out of the Jaylen Brown business enabled it to accomplish so much: getting a motivated All-Star feeling the sting of rejection following a career year, dumping George's contract and putting themselves in position to be attractive to an all-time great in James, who was looking for a new challenge. They also lessened their dependency on Joel Embiid's bothersome health as he will turn 33 during the season.

They filled in the blanks by adding Caldwell-Pope and Wade as plug-and-play wings, changing the complexion of their franchise in several swoops. If nothing else, they won the offseason. -- Vincent Goodwill

Read the full offseason recap/season preview

Boston Celtics: Sept. 15

Brooklyn Nets: Sept. 16

Toronto Raptors: Sept. 17

New York Knicks: Sept. 18

Central Division

Milwaukee Bucks: Sept. 7
Key additions: Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis, Caris LeVert

Key retentions: Gary Trent Jr.

Key subtractions: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Bobby Portis

After 13 seasons, the Giannis era ended in Milwaukee with a mega trade to the Heat -- and the 2026-27 season will mark a major shift for the rebuilding franchise.

The Bucks hired coach Taylor Jenkins to establish a culture. They added four new players from Miami, including former All-Star and Wisconsin native Tyler Herro, and selected Brayden Burries with the No. 10 pick in June.

The Bucks will enter the season with an ill-fitting mix of players and low expectations, but they have the luxury to see what sticks long term. -- Jamal Collier

Read the full Bucks offseason recap/season preview

Chicago Bulls: Sept. 8
Key additions: F Caleb Wilson, G Dailyn Swain, C Nic Claxton, G Norman Powell, Tiago Splitter

Key subtractions: None

Key retentions: F Zach Collins

For years, Chicago has been seen as one of the sleeping giants of the NBA, a once-proud franchise reduced to meandering in the play-in tournament and in the middle of the lottery in recent seasons. But the Bulls got a much-needed makeover this summer and enter the 2026-27 season with a clearer direction than they've had in years.

The changes have been full-scale: Bryson Graham was hired as the team's new head of basketball operations, Tiago Splitter will patrol the sidelines as head coach, No. 4 pick Caleb Wilson is the new face of the franchise, and he'll be surrounded by some veterans like Nic Claxton and Norman Powell to help ease his transition. -- Jamal Collier

Read the full Bulls offseason recap/season preview

Cleveland Cavaliers: Sept. 9
Key additions: Peyton Watson, Mario Hezonja

Key subtractions: Dean Wade, Dennis Schroder, Max Strus, Larry Nance Jr., Caris Levert, Keon Ellis

Key retentions: Donovan Mitchell, James Harden

The Cavs' failed pursuit of LeBron James this summer turned into a pivot for a younger, athletic wing, prying Watson from the Nuggets after a career-year.

Watson averaged career highs in points, rebounds, assists and steals while shooting 41% from 3 last year, and he has in recent years been one of the strongest wing defenders in the league. That makes him a strong complement next to James Harden and Donovan Mitchell, as the Cavs hope he can provide a substantial answer to the elusive fifth starter role next to their core four. -- Jamal Collier

Read the full Cavaliers offseason recap/season preview

Detroit Pistons: Sept. 10
Key additions: John Collins, Isaiah Joe, Taurean Prince, Gary Harris

Key subtractions: Tobias Harris, Isaiah Stewart

Key retentions: None

The Pistons' offseason is still in limbo as negotiations with restricted free agent Jalen Duren have stalled.

Detroit believes it sent Duren a fair offer considering the totality of his 2025-26 season -- including his underwhelming playoff showing -- while Duren feels like he's checked off all the boxes to get more.

Losing Harris and Stewart will be a big test to their culture -- or a signal they have to win a different way than in the last two seasons.

They added shooting on the margins with Joe, Prince and Harris. And assuming Duren's deal gets done before camp, Ausar Thompson's contract is next on the docket. -- Vincent Goodwill

Read the full Pistons offseason recap/season preview

Indiana Pacers: Sept. 11
Key additions: Kelly Oubre Jr., Larry Nance Jr.

Key retentions: None

Key subtractions: C Micah Potter

The Pacers didn't make any major offseason changes, but they will have two major additions to the roster they were missing last year: starting center Ivica Zubac, who was acquired at the trade deadline from the Clippers, and star guard Tyrese Haliburton, returning from injury for the first time since the 2025 NBA Finals.

Haliburton's presence lifted the Pacers into an Eastern Conference contender in 2024 and '25, and 16 months after a torn Achilles, they'll be counting on him to do the same in 2027. And Zubac will provide a different kind of center than Myles Turner provided the last time Haliburton was on the court. -- Jamal Collier

Read the full offseason recap/season preview

Southeast Division

Miami Heat: Aug. 31
Key additions: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Klay Thompson, Bobby Portis, Tim Hardaway Jr., Nick Richards

Key retentions: Andrew Wiggins, Simone Fontecchio

Key subtractions: Tyler Herro, Norman Powell, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis

Heat president Pat Riley landed the superstar he'd been searching for since LeBron James left Miami in 2016. Antetokounmpo is in the fold, and Miami is ready to contend for another title with the two-time MVP. Antetokounmpo is just as motivated to win his second title and remind everyone that he can be the best player in the league.

In the trade, the Heat gave up key players such as Herro, Ware and Jaquez and did not bring back Powell in free agency. They landed Thompson to a two-year, $13 million deal after the four-time champion sharpshooter worked out a buyout with the Dallas Mavericks. Miami also added Portis and Hardaway, but the team is still looking to bolster the roster around Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Heat offseason recap/season preview

Washington Wizards: Sept. 1
Key additions: AJ Dybantsa, Khris Middleton, Deandre Ayton, Tre Mann

Key subtractions: Cam Whitmore, D'Angelo Russell, Jaden Hardy

Key retentions: Trae Young

The Wizards got their jump on this pivotal offseason by acquiring Trae Young and Anthony Davis last season in trades.

Those were their two big moves and then came the big prize for losing 65 games last season - winning the lottery and drafting AJ Dybantsa with the first overall pick.

Ready to start winning games this season after losing 60 or more games in each of the past three years, Washington gave Young a four-year, $212 million contract. The Wizards added veterans like Khris Middleton and Deandre Ayton to bolster the depth behind their young core featuring the likes of Dybantsa, Alex Sarr, Kyshawn George, Tre Johnson and Will Riley. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Wizards offseason recap/season preview

Charlotte Hornets: Sept. 2
Key additions: F Naz Reid, G Grayson Allen, G Dennis Schroder, F Royce O'Neale, F Dorian Finney-Smith

Key retentions: G Coby White

Key subtractions: G LaMelo Ball, F Miles Bridges, G Josh Green, G Tre Mann

After enjoying their best season in a decade, the Hornets sharply changed course with the surprising decision to trade Ball, their franchise guard, to the Timberwolves.

Given that Ball was a borderline All-Star on a max contract, Charlotte opted for a "Moneyball" approach in hopes of avoiding the perpetual mediocrity that tripped up Trae Young's Atlanta Hawks in the recent past.

With Ball and starting forward Miles Bridges moved in separate deals aimed at collecting future draft assets and improving its cap flexibility, Charlotte is now the only team that doesn't have a single player on the books for at least $25 million next season. -- Ben Golliver

Read the full Hornets offseason recap/season preview

Atlanta Hawks: Sept. 3
Key additions: Luguentz Dort, Aaron Wiggins, Kingston Flemings, Devin Carter, Ryan Nembhard, Zuby Ejiofor, Henri Veesaar

Key retentions: CJ McCollum, Jock Landale

Key subtractions: Zaccharie Risacher, Jonathan Kuminga, Gabe Vincent, Keaton Wallace

Atlanta continued to move forward from the Trae Young trade last season by being opportunistic this offseason.

The Hawks acquired Dort and Wiggins in separate trades from the Oklahoma City Thunder to add more help around emerging star Jalen Johnson. The Hawks also kept McCollum on a one-year, $21 million deal and drafted Flemings eighth overall.

Atlanta is loaded with young wings looking to take a step forward under Quin Snyder like Nickeil Alexander-Walker did last season in winning Most Improved Player. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Hawks offseason recap/season preview

Orlando Magic: Sept. 4
Key additions: C Nikola Vucevic, G Izaiyah Nelson

Key subtractions: F Moritz Wagner, G Jett Howard

Key retentions: F Jonathan Isaac, G Jevon Carter

The Magic's biggest move this offseason was hiring Sean Sweeney to replace Jamahl Mosley.

Orlando also brought Nikola Vucevic back on a one-year, $3.9 million deal since trading him in 2021 and will use his ability to score and shoot to space the floor for Paolo Banchero, Franz Wagner and Desmond Bane.

The Magic blew a 3-1 lead over top-seeded Detroit in the first round of the playoffs after Wagner went down due to injury and were in desperate need of someone who can get easier baskets and make outside shots. Vucevic should help. Moe Wagner departed for Brooklyn via free agency, separating Franz from his brother for the first time in his pro career. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Magic offseason recap/season preview

Pacific Division

Los Angeles Lakers: Aug. 24
Key additions: C Walker Kessler, F Sandro Mamukelashvili, G Quentin Grimes, G Collin Sexton, F Kevon Looney, F Matisse Thybulle, G Cameron Carr

Key retentions: G Austin Reaves

Key subtractions: F LeBron James, C Deandre Ayton, G Marcus Smart, F Rui Hachimura, G Luke Kennard, C Jaxson Hayes

James informed the Lakers he would not be returning for next season on June 30. Two days later, the team transformed the roster, with Doncic squarely as the focal point.

The biggest addition -- literally and figuratively -- is 7-foot-2 center Kessler, acquired in a sign-and-trade deal with the Utah Jazz. L.A. sent two unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033 and pick swaps in 2028 and 2030, not to mention a four-year, $130 million contract, to acquire him.

Mamukelashvili, Grimes, Sexton, Looney and Thybulle also signed with the Lakers, and free agent Ziaire Williams and first-round pick Carr bolster the team's young prospect pool of Adou Thiero, Bronny James and Dalton Knecht.

The most important move, though, came when Reaves, coming off a career season in which he averaged 23.3 points, 4.7 rebounds and 5.5 assists per game, signed a four-year, $180 million extension.

When the dust settled, it was a dramatic roster overhaul in what could prove to be one of the most consequential summers in franchise history, with the team also being sold for the second time in 14 months, this time to venture capitalist Josh Kushner and former Disney CEO Bob Iger, who bought the Lakers from Mark Walter at a $12.5 billion valuation. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Lakers offseason recap/season preview

LA Clippers: Aug. 25
Key additions: Rui Hachimura, Keaton Wagler, Brandon Ingram (TBD), Gradey Dick (TBD)

Key retentions: Kobe Sanders, Bradley Beal

Key subtractions: Kawhi Leonard (TBD), Nicolas Batum, Bogdan Bogdanovic, John Collins

What started as a reconfiguration at the trade deadline -- acquiring Darius Garland from Cleveland for James Harden and Bennedict Mathurin from Indiana for Ivica Zubac -- turned into a complete overhaul this summer after the Clippers let Bogdan Bogdanovic, Nicolas Batum and John Collins walk.

Their biggest move, however, was trading Leonard to the Toronto Raptors for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick and draft picks, but that deal is in limbo pending the investigation into alleged salary cap circumvention by the team relating to Leonard's Aspiration endorsement deal.

In the meantime, LA added Illinois guard Wagler with the No. 5 pick in the draft and signed Hachimura away from the crosstown Lakers with a two-year, $28 million deal. And in a surprise move, Bradley Beal -- after declining his $5.6 million contract option for next season in June to test free agency -- ended up re-signing on a two-year, $13.2 million deal in mid-August to stay with the Clippers. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Clippers offseason recap/season preview

Golden State Warriors: Aug. 26
Key additions: Yaxel Lendeborg, Brandon Williams, Georges Niang

Key subtractions: Quinten Post, Pat Spencer

Key retentions: Draymond Green, Al Horford, Kristaps Porzingis, Gary Payton II, De'Anthony Melton

The Warriors opted for flexibility and stability over a larger shake-up around Curry. Their much-publicized recruitment of James never gained much traction.

They brought back their veteran frontcourt trio (Green, Horford, Porzingis), but kept them all on short-term maneuverable contracts. They opted for the fit of Melton over a pursuit of scoring guard Anfernee Simons. Their big addition is Lendeborg, the 23-year-old rookie wing who they will rely upon to be a high-minute, high-impact rotation player immediately.

In the bigger picture, they protected their draft pick cupboard and lined up their books to have an ocean of cap space as they peer a bit deeper into the future while their core ages. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Warriors offseason recap/season preview

Phoenix Suns: Aug. 27
Key additions: F Miles Bridges, F Koa Peat, G Luke Kennard

Key subtractions: G Grayson Allen, F Royce O'Neale

Key retentions: F Dillon Brooks, G Collin Gillespie, C Mark Williams, G Jordan Goodwin

Phoenix followed up its surprising season with a series of moves to mostly keep its team intact, with some adjustments around the margins.

The Suns re-signed Gillespie (four years, $48 million), Williams (three years, $38 million), Goodwin (three years, $19 million) and Brooks (three years, $73 million) to new deals and made a major splash by trading Allen and O'Neale to the Charlotte Hornets for Bridges. And despite not having a pick until No. 47 in the second round of the 2026 draft, Phoenix was able to acquire Arizona player Peat -- who averaged 14.1 points on 52.8% shooting as a freshman for the Wildcats and was key to their Final Four run. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Suns offseason recap/season preview

Sacramento Kings: Aug. 28
Key additions: G Darius Acuff Jr., F Alex Karaban, G Emanuel Sharp

Key subtractions: G DeMar DeRozan, G Russell Westbrook

Key retentions: F Precious Achiuwa

Perry, currently in the organization's power seat, is continuing a steady transition toward the younger core he has drafted. Arkansas guard and No. 7 pick Acuff is the spotlight name on a roster populated with six players in their first two NBA seasons.

But they still have notable high-minute holdovers from the past regime, including Murray, Malik Monk, LaVine and Sabonis. Of those four, Murray appears the most locked-in as a stable member of the team's long-term vision. Perry explored trades for Monk, LaVine and Sabonis over the past year, but didn't value the proposed returns, and the three are expected to open the season in Sacramento. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Kings offseason recap/season preview

Northwest Division

Portland Trail Blazers: Aug. 17
Key additions: G Ja Morant, F Jeremy Sochan

Key retentions: C Robert Williams III

Key subtractions: F Jerami Grant, F Kris Murray, G Matisse Thybulle

Sadly, the Blazers made far more noise this offseason with their off-court business dealings than anything they did with their roster. New owner Tom Dundon's aggressive cost-cutting measures and ongoing fight for arena financing have distracted from the progress that Portland made on the court last season, when it reached the playoffs for the first time since 2021.

Although the Blazers were the only team that sat out June's draft by not making a pick, they will add two high-profile guards to a rotation that otherwise looks very similar to last season. Lillard, a franchise icon, is back from an Achilles tendon injury that sidelined him for the entire 2025-26 campaign, and Morant, a two-time All-Star, arrived in a trade that sent Grant and Murray to the Memphis Grizzlies. -- Ben Golliver

Read the full Blazers offseason recap/season preview

Utah Jazz: Aug. 18
Key additions: G Darryn Peterson, C Jaxson Hayes, G Josh Okogie

Key retentions: C Jusuf Nurkic

Key subtractions: C Walker Kessler

The Jazz finally got some lottery luck, landing at No. 2 and taking Peterson, a gifted guard who has the potential to emerge as the face of the franchise. The hope was that Peterson would be the final major piece in Utah's rebuild, but that plan featured Kessler as the team's long-term starting center. Instead, the Jazz agreed to a sign-and-trade deal that sent Kessler to the Lakers in exchange for a pair of future first-round picks and two swaps.

The return was widely considered to be great value for Utah, particularly after Kessler's deal (four years, $130 million) pushed beyond the Jazz's comfort zone, but there is now a glaring need in the starting lineup alongside Jackson and Lauri Markkanen in the frontcourt. -- Tim MacMahon

Read the full Jazz offseason recap/season preview

Minnesota Timberwolves: Aug. 19
Key additions: G LaMelo Ball, G Josh Green, G Isaiah Evans

Key subtractions: F Julius Randle, C Naz Reid

Key retentions: G Ayo Dosunmu, G Bones Hyland, G Jaylen Clark

Wolves president of basketball operations Tim Connelly continued to show his aggression, orchestrating a four-team trade with the Brooklyn Nets, Chicago Bulls and Charlotte Hornets that sent out three-time All-Star Randle and the 2023-24 Sixth Man of the Year, Reid, and a future first-round pick to bring in the talented -- but polarizing -- Ball.

That move followed Connelly inking 6-foot-4 guard Dosunmu to a five-year, $112 million extension in June, following his acquisition at the deadline.

Minnesota also re-signed wing Clark and guard Hyland and acquired the 6-foot-6 Evans out of Duke with the No. 33 pick in the draft.

Coach Chris Finch also lost his top lieutenant on the bench, Micah Nori, who left to coach the Portland Trail Blazers. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Timberwolves offseason recap/season preview

Oklahoma City Thunder: Aug. 20
Key additions: C Aday Mara, G Bennett Stirtz

Key retentions: G Kenrich Williams, C Isaiah Hartenstein

Key subtractions: G Isaiah Joe, G Aaron Wiggins, G Luguentz Dort

The extensions for both Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren triggered in July, leading to a trio of financially motivated trades to slash the tax bill and cost-control the current roster.

They sent Isaiah Joe to Detroit and traded Aaron Wiggins and Lu Dort to Atlanta in separate moves, eroding their depth.

General manager Sam Presti made clear in an interview with The Oklahoman that the impression he's been given from ownership is "the savings generated this summer, and from being out of the tax the last several years, will be re-allocated to future teams."

That would mean extra breathing room to eventually extend core young players such as Cason Wallace and Ajay Mitchell. Wallace, the likely replacement starter for Dort, is extension eligible off his rookie contract into October. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Thunder offseason recap/season preview

Denver Nuggets: Aug. 21
Key additions: Marvin Bagley III, Lonnie Walker IV

Key retentions: Spencer Jones, Tyus Jones

Key subtractions: Watson, Tim Hardaway Jr., Jonas Valanciunas

Finding a resolution to Watson's restricted free agency was Denver's most important piece of summer business.

Watson is a draft success story, rising from the 30th overall pick into one of the league's more intriguing young two-way wings. But retaining the 23-year-old would have been expensive -- via either a sky-high luxury tax bill or a salary-slashing move to get off an important veteran and generate more breathing room for a new deal.

After Wednesday's deal to send Watson to Cleveland, Denver's front office can shift its attention to escaping the salary cap's second apron. The Nuggets are currently the league's only team above it. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Nuggets offseason recap/season preview

Southwest Division

Memphis Grizzlies: Aug. 14
Key additions: F Cameron Boozer, G D'Angelo Russell, F Isaiah Stewart, F Jerami Grant, F Kris Murray, C Quinten Post

Key retentions: None

Key subtractions: G Ja Morant, F Santi Aldama

Memphis finally traded Ja Morant, turning the last page from an ultimately disappointing chapter in franchise history, and already has his replacement as the face of the franchise in place: No. 3 pick Cameron Boozer. GM Zach Kleiman has overhauled the roster in the past few transaction cycles, acquiring four first-round picks when he traded Desmond Bane, a few more when he dealt Jaren Jackson Jr. and none for Morant, whose departure signaled a fresh start for the Grizzlies and him.

Memphis is in a full-blown youth movement, as 21-year-old forward GG Jackson is now the longest-tenured player on the roster. The Grizzlies say they believe they have a long-term foundation in place with their last few lottery picks: center Zach Edey, small forward Cedric Coward and power forward Boozer. -- Tim MacMahon

Read the full Grizzlies offseason recap/season preview

New Orleans Pelicans: Aug. 13
Key additions: None

Key retentions: C DeAndre Jordan

Key subtractions: F Kevon Looney

Despite capturing a combined 47 wins over the last two seasons under executive vice president Joe Dumars and general manager Troy Weaver, the Pelicans clearly believe that internal growth is the best path forward. Perhaps that justifies a near-silent summer in which the hiring of new coach Jamahl Mosley turned out to be the team's most notable move. Mosley becomes New Orleans' third coach since Dumars took the helm in April 2025. In addition to drafting Jaron Pierre Jr. in the second round, New Orleans signed just two new players over the summer in Kobe Bufkin and Hunter Dickinson, while bringing back 14 of the 15 players from last season's squad. -- Michael C. Wright

Read the full Pelicans offseason recap/season preview

Dallas Mavericks: Aug. 12
Key additions: F Morez Johnson Jr., F Zaccharie Risacher

Key retentions: Moussa Cisse

Key subtractions: Khris Middleton, Ryan Nembhard

The major changes made by the Mavericks this offseason were in the managerial and coaching ranks. After a seasonlong search, team governor Patrick Dumont hired Masai Ujiri to run the franchise's basketball operations, bringing the architect of the Toronto Raptors' 2019 title team to Dallas. Ujiri decided to part ways with coach Jason Kidd and recruited Dusty May, fresh off an NCAA title with Michigan, to replace him.

Johnson, who played for May at Michigan before the Mavs selected him with the No. 9 pick in the draft, is the headliner of the additions to the roster. Dallas added three potential immediate contributors in a six-team deal, acquiring former Grizzlies forward Santi Aldama, ex-Pistons guard Marcus Sasser and EuroLeague veteran Tarik Biberovic. The franchise also landed former No. 1 pick as part of the trade that sent Luguentz Dort from the Oklahoma City Thunder to the Atlanta Hawks. -- MacMahon

Read the full Mavericks offseason recap/season preview

Houston Rockets: Aug. 11
Key additions: G Marcus Smart, G Bogdan Bogdanovic

Key retentions: F Tari Eason

Key subtractions: F Dorian Finney-Smith, G Josh Okogie

After suffering a first-round postseason exit for the second consecutive season, the Rockets resisted the temptation to jump into the Giannis Antetokounmpo sweepstakes after adding former MVP Durant last summer. General manager Rafael Stone and coach Ime Udoka will instead lean on growth from the team's collection of young talent acquired in recent years, not to mention the continuity that comes with those players developing together over multiple seasons.

Houston signed Tari Eason to a five-year, $81.5 million extension over the summer. But outside of that, the Rockets focused on bolstering depth by bringing aboard veterans Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanovic. The club also brought in renowned shooting coach Chip Engelland from Oklahoma City. Engelland spent more than a decade with the San Antonio Spurs, winning two titles. -- Wright

Read the full Rockets offseason recap/season preview

San Antonio Spurs: Aug. 10
Key additions: F Tobias Harris

Key retentions: F Harrison Barnes

Key subtractions: None

San Antonio's surprising run to the NBA Finals never obscured its long-term vision for building a sustainable competitor around Victor Wembanyama. Clearly, the Frenchman views the future similarly, considering he signed a 25% max extension worth $252 million instead of the available 30% supermax escalators that would've rocketed the contract to $303 million.

Wembanyama did it to keep San Antonio's talented young core together for as long as possible, with added flexibility to acquire needed supporting players. The Spurs grabbed one of those in free agency in Harris, an experienced, reliable scorer who adds size (6-foot-8, 226 pounds) and physicality on defense while bolstering frontcourt depth in the draft. -- Wright

Read the full Spurs offseason recap/season preview

stories.headline: Honda replacing F1 engine chief after poor start to return with Aston Martin
stories.summary: Honda is replacing the head of its Formula 1 power unit project following the manufacturer's disappointing start to 2026 as Aston Martin's engine supplier.
stories.body:
Honda is replacing the head of its Formula 1 power unit project following the manufacturer's disappointing start to 2026 as Aston Martin's engine supplier.

In what the company calls a "planned transition," Yoichiro Fukao will take over the lead role in Honda's F1 power unit project from Tetsushi Kakuda on Oct. 1.

Fukao is currently the deputy leader of Honda's power unit project and has worked for the company since 2002 in positions in F1, MotoGP and mass production.

Honda joined forces with Aston Martin at the start of this season, but has struggled for performance under F1's new power unit regulations.

"This organisational change is a planned transition designed to ensure the reliable transfer of technical expertise to the next generation of engineers," a Honda statement said.

"Following the introduction of the new regulations in 2026, and with further regulatory changes expected from 2027 onwards, Honda aims to establish a robust development framework and deliver a highly competitive PU by transitioning to the new structure at an early stage."

The Japanese manufacturer had enjoyed a period of success with Red Bull under the previous set of power unit regulations, which included Max Verstappen taking four drivers' titles with Honda power.

However, a significant number of the staff that worked on the previous power unit design left the project in 2021 after Honda initially announced its intention to end its involvement in F1 at the end of the 2025 season.

- Spanish Grand Prix: Kimi Antonelli wins again as Lando Norris rues bad luck, Lewis Hamilton suffers DNF

- Lando Norris hits out at F1 Virtual Safety Car rule after losing 'deserved' Spanish GP win

- Madring's F1 debut left everyone dissatisfied, even Spanish GP's top 3

A shift in F1's regulations for 2026 to ensure 50 percent of the power unit's overall output came from the battery convinced Honda to continue in F1, but its early development under the new rules stalled due to its earlier decision to disband its power unit department.

Both Honda and Aston Martin started the season on the back foot, and the team has scored just three points all season, leaving it 10th in the constructors' standings

Honda introduced an engine upgrade at the Dutch Grand Prix by using one of the development steps afforded by F1's catch-up mechanism, ADUO, but remains adrift of its rivals.

stories.headline: U.S. beats France for fifth straight women's World Cup title
stories.summary: Team USA largely credited Breanna Stewart for helping guide them to the program's fifth straight World Cup title after a win over France in the final.
stories.body:
BERLIN -- For the first time in years, maybe decades, Team USA looked vulnerable entering and even during the 2026 women's basketball World Cup.

Veterans A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum were late scratches heading into the tournament. France, which nearly beat the U.S. at the Olympics in 2024, was out for blood. A three-point win against Italy in the group phase and a close call against Spain in the semifinals only made the outside noise intensify heading into Sunday's gold medal match.

The feeling was that maybe Team USA would miss out on gold at a major international tournament for the first time since 2006 and only the second time since 1994.

But as team captain Breanna Stewart sat in the news conference following Saturday's semifinal, previewing the final showdown against France, she exuded a quiet confidence.

"I've been in these games," she said at the time. "The emotional part of it is really what's going to teeter teams [for things] to not go their way. And my team, we're going to be locked in. We're going to be very composed. Doesn't matter what happens to us, we know that it's going to be a long game."

About 24 hours later, Stewart sat back in that very spot with an American flag draped around her and a gold medal around her neck, fresh off leading USA to a 97-79 victory over France. Her 22-point, 10-rebound performance in the final helped her earn World Cup MVP honors.

"I pride myself on being consistent, and that's showing up when it's the big moments and the small moments and all the moments in between," Stewart said. "It's like an unrealistic confidence that I have in myself, especially in those big moments. I believe that I always have a chance to win no matter what happens in the game."

Stewart further solidified her argument as arguably the winningest player in the sport's history, boasting four NCAA championships, three WNBA titles, three Olympic gold medals and now four World Cup golds, tying Sue Bird for the most of all time.

"It starts with Stewie," coach Kara Lawson said. "Her leadership, not just tonight, throughout the whole tournament, helping to guide the younger players, talk to them, just show them what it looks like to win.

"She is USA Basketball. When you think of the last 15 years, it's Stewie, and we're just really lucky to be a part of her era of this group."

Stewart has been a stalwart with USA Basketball for over a decade and in recent years has taken the reins alongside Wilson as pillars of this era of Team USA. But her on-court productivity and leadership had never been more important than in Berlin. The team was left with just three players -- Stewart, Chelsea Gray and Kahleah Copper -- who'd played in a World Cup before, a tournament many say is harder to win than the Olympics. Seven of the 12 had never even suited up for the senior national team in a major tournament.

Stewart ultimately led Team USA in scoring (12.8 points per game), rebounds (7.3 RPG) and efficiency rating (18.8), anchoring the defense and often even playing point guard if that's what the game required. She had her fingerprints all over the France win between a crucial 12 points in the first half to keep the USA afloat and timely plays that helped the team pull away after halftime.

"The thing that I appreciate about her the most is her willingness to do anything to help the team," Lawson said. "It's so rare in a player of her caliber.

"She will play any position for us to win, and that quality is why she's the greatest winner that we've had, probably."

Her most important contribution might have come off the court. She was the standard-bearer tasked with ensuring that this younger generation understands the expectations that come with representing the U.S. And she also had to help them navigate the pressure that comes with that.

In the weight room after the team barely beat Italy in its second game -- in what would have been one of the most shocking results the sport had seen in years -- Stewart noticed several younger players had a look of "what just happened" on their faces. She shared with them how heading into the 2014 World Cup, her first, USA lost to France in an exhibition but still went on to win the tournament.

"Stewie's been a tremendous leader through this whole process for us," Caitlin Clark said after the gold medal game. "Even after we had that close game with Italy, she was somebody that was really vocal in the locker room about, 'Don't be flustered by this. This is normal for a World Cup. You're going to have to kind of get it out of the mud at some points. It's not always going to be pretty.'"

The team's ability to internalize her message and stay the course was crucial for the remainder of the tournament, and perhaps in no situation more than when France jumped ahead by 14 in the second quarter. It was the first double-digit deficit Team USA faced in a World Cup game since the 2006 semifinal, the program's last loss in the event.

"Our group, our starters especially, when we got down big, we didn't crumble under pressure," Stewart said about the team's ability to cut the deficit to two going into halftime and then respond with a 30-12 third quarter. "[France's] run wasn't going to dictate how we were going to play the rest of the game."

Added Clark: "Stewie's a winner. All she ever does is win. She's been in so many of these moments, and when you have somebody like that on your team, it's just a really comforting thing."

Stewart didn't do it all alone -- fellow veterans Chelsea Gray, Young, Copper and Napheesa Collier also came up big against France -- but her peers recognize how special Stewart is.

"She's so skilled, man. I think sometimes you get used to seeing excellence all the time and you get complacent," said Gray, who has faced off against Stewart many times competing for WNBA championships. "You see the way she competes, the way she finishes the ball, the way she brings the team together. Things like this don't happen by accident.

"We've done it together a few times and I'm happy to share the court with her."

Added Paige Bueckers: "To see [her operate] up close and personal, it was definitely eye-opening."

The keys to USA Basketball will eventually be handed over to the likes of Bueckers, Clark, Angel Reese and Aliyah Boston, all of whom have now learned from and won with Stewart.

But as far as she's concerned, Stewart doesn't want to be done with USA Basketball -- and winning on the biggest of stages -- anytime soon.

Asked on the television broadcast if she can run it back with this group at the Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028, Stewart responded, "Oh yeah, see you in L.A.!"

stories.headline: Fenerbahce coach returns to work after resignation confusion
stories.summary: Fenerbahce coach Ismail Kartal returned to his duties on Saturday, contradicting media reports from the day before suggesting his resignation was final.
stories.body:
ISTANBUL -- Fenerbahce coach Ismail Kartal returned to his duties on Saturday, contradicting media reports from the day before suggesting his resignation was final.

Kartal had announced he was quitting his role following Thursday's draw against AS Roma in the Champions League but the club refused to accept his resignation.

Kartal, nevertheless, failed to attend training on Friday ahead of a Superlig game against Gaziantep FK.

However, Fenerbahce released a statement late Friday saying Kartal would resume his duties on Saturday for the Super Lig match against Gaziantep on Monday.

On Saturday, the club's official X account showed photos of him at work.

Kartal had resigned to the surprise of the club and its players in his news conference following the 1-1 draw with Roma to begin the Turkish club's Champions League season.

"First of all, I congratulate my players for carrying out the tasks I assigned for tonight's match to the letter. We played football worthy of the Champions League," the state-run Anadolu Agency quoted Kartal as saying on Thursday. "We could have won the match; we had clear chances. The match ended in a draw, and I am proud of my players."

Kartal continued: "Tonight, I am resigning from my position -- never to return. I extend my heartfelt thanks to my players."

In a separate news conference soon after, club chairman Aziz Yildirim said Fenerbahce fans had hurled a water bottle at Kartal, describing the incident as a reason for the coach's decision. Kartal was also upset by a series of social media posts, Yildirim said.

Yildirim insisted that Kartal's resignation was not accepted and that he would remain at the helm.

"You saw the state Ismail was in. Can a person endure that much distress?" Yildirim said. "They threw a water bottle at Ismail Kartal's head. We saw it. That is why he is upset."

"Ismail Kartal remains in his post," Yildirim added. "I said [to Kartal]: 'You will continue,' and that was that."

Despite reports in Turkey that Fenerbahce official Oguz Cetin later met with Kartal but failed to convince him to stay, Kartal is now set to take charge of the team's fixture against Gaziantep FK on Monday.

Fenerbahce is 11th in the 18-team league.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

stories.body:
LAS VEGAS -- Golden Knights captain Mark Stone signed a two-year contract extension Saturday with a $9 million annual value that goes through the 2028-29 season.

He will make $9.5 million this season in the final year of his current deal.

Stone, 34, is coming off a season in which he totaled a career-high 73 points (28 goals, 45 assists) for a Golden Knights team that advanced to the Stanley Cup Final before losing to the Carolina Hurricanes in six games.

Known for boisterous goal celebrations, Stone is the emotional driver behind the Golden Knights, having played in 400 career games for the club. He also has produced, scoring 136 goals with 260 assists and a +112 rating.

Stone has 259 goals and 448 assists over a 15-year career, including more than six seasons with Ottawa before his trade to Vegas on Feb. 25, 2019.

Injuries have kept Stone from delivering even more, but he has played in at least 60 games each of the past two seasons. If Stone can stay healthy, especially going into the playoffs, the Golden Knights could make another deep postseason run with roster that includes Jack Eichel and Mitch Marner.

stories.headline: Cleary avoids ban, but drama far from over
stories.summary: Penrith's hopes of a fifth premiership in six years could again hinge on Nathan Cleary's fitness, after his joy at avoiding a finals ban was dampened by confirmation of bone damage in his foot.
stories.body:
Penrith's hopes of a fifth premiership in six years could again hinge on Nathan Cleary's fitness, after his joy at avoiding a finals ban was dampened by confirmation of bone damage in his foot.

Cleary was on Monday handed a grade-one dangerous contact charge for collecting Hugo Savala's leg after the Sydney Rooster kicked in Penrith's 19-12 qualifying-final win.

That charge only carries with it a $1000 fine with an early guilty plea, meaning Cleary can breathe a sigh of relief with no ban.

But the bigger issue is now Cleary's foot, after Penrith confirmed he had "sustained a stress-related bone issue in his foot".

Cleary had appeared to tell a Panthers physio it was "f---ed" soon after kicking his match-winning field goal in Sunday's victory.

The two-time Clive Churchill Medallist had scans on Monday, with Penrith now tight-lipped on Cleary's exact path forward..

"Cleary will continue to be assessed and monitored by the Panthers medical team," the Panthers said in a statement.

It would likely take astronomical damage for Cleary to miss Penrith's preliminary final, or grand final if they again win through to the decider.

The Panthers have the best part of two weeks to rest up before taking on the Warriors or Newcastle, and the star halfback could take a pain-killing injection if required.

Penrith are also no strangers to having men play through injury in vital games.

Cleary's co-captain Isaah Yeo is playing this finals series after delaying surgery on a ruptured pec, while fullback Dylan Edwards soldiered on with a broken foot in 2021.

Cleary himself battled on after a dislocated shoulder in 2021, and needed shoulder surgery again when Penrith lifted their fourth straight title in 2024.

READ: NRL 2026 team-by-team season review

Penrith's title runs have often hinged on Cleary's foot. His kicking has been key in all four of premierships.

But the bigger question would likely be how much the injury or any treatment impacts Cleary's ability to run, step and kick through the rest of this finals series.

In the unlikely event Cleary is out, Penrith have Jack Cogger returning from suspension for the preliminary final, with Jack Cole having been solid at No.6.

Blaize Talagi could also return to the halves. He filled in at centre on Sunday after being dropped last month.

"It's incredible the depth we have," second-rower Liam Martin said.

"Jack's (Cole) been unbelievable the last three weeks. His defence has been incredibly strong, his attack, his running game.

"He's playing with such confidence. It's awesome to see. He's always had the talent and worked hard. I'm really glad to see him get his chance."

Meanwhile, the match review committee's call to hand Cleary a grade-one charge saved Penrith weighing up a monumental decision.

Had Cleary been handed a grade-two charge, the Penrith halfback would have been facing a one-game ban and the reality of being rubbed out of the preliminary final.

If Penrith had fought the charge and lost, that ban would have extended to the grand final.

Manly prop Josh Aloiai and South Sydney forward Jacob Host received grade-two charges in 2024 for making contact with kickers.

Canberra's Zac Hosking was fined for a similar incident in last year's finals, while Melbourne's Harry Grant had a charge overturned at the judiciary in 2024.

Speaking before Cleary escaped with a fine, Cronulla half Nicho Hynes called for consistency.

"Sometimes people get suspended for it, sometimes you won't," Hynes said.

"I love Nathan and he's a really good guy and you don't want to see your best players getting stamped out of the final series.

"But whatever's warranted is warranted. As long as it's equal for every player across the board, then that's all that matters.

"You've got to treat everyone the same, regardless of whether you're the face of the game or you're not."
