stories.headline: Broncos using the same formula as the 2015 Super Bowl team?
stories.summary: The 2015 Broncos used a united front office, shutdown defense and clutch play to win Super Bowl 50. And the 2026 Broncos have a similar makeup -- and goal.
stories.body:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- When Aqib Talib looks at the current version of the Denver Broncos, he sees a reflection of his football past.

"They're us," the former Pro Bowl cornerback said when comparing the current Broncos to the franchise's Super Bowl 50 championship team. "They all love ball, talk to each other, hold each other to it. It's clear as day when you see it."

Talib is not the only player from the Broncos' most recent Super Bowl-winning team to see history potentially repeating itself. Dallas Cowboys edge rusher Von Miller -- who was the MVP of the Broncos' Super Bowl win over the Carolina Panthers at the end of the 2015 season -- feels a similar vibe with the 2026 Broncos.

"Oh yeah, I see it," Miller said earlier this summer. "They do it the way we did it. ... You can tell they keep it straight with each other."

This is turn-back-the-clock stuff for Talib, Miller and those who lived it in 2015. They see similarities between how their championship team was set up and how the current Broncos, who were 14-3 last season and went to the AFC Championship Game, function. The two teams share parallels on and off the field, including institutional support, reliance on an elite-level defense and a penchant for thriving in close games. And these Broncos now hope that the culture created from this formula gets them a Super Bowl win, just like the 2015 team. Denver begins its quest for its fourth title when it plays at the Kansas City Chiefs on "Monday Night Football" (8:15 p.m. ET, ESPN/ABC).

"Real winning is in what you might not even see until it's right," Talib said. "It's that attitude, that giving and sharing. You give everything you have, and you don't ever lower that bar on anything, and you hold each other to it every day. And you get guys who can take that accountability. They have it, we had it."

When Broncos coach Sean Payton is asked a question about winning, his responses start with words like program, grit and culture. He believes this roster has those things, which is why 45 of the players who were on the 53-man roster for last season's opener still remain with the franchise.

That rate of retention is almost unheard of in the NFL and is risky in its own way. But Payton believed this group was good enough to be in the Super Bowl hunt last season because of how it was assembled -- and believes it is good enough again.

"Culture is one of those things, we all talk about it, it's like a go-to word sometimes, but to really have it ... it's rare I think," Broncos defensive tackle Zach Allen said. "Some places just say they have it and it's really nowhere to be found. ... If you need to be pushed, or reminded to work, or, like be told to get to work, you're not going to be around here."

'Finding the right people'
Payton has often said that the number of NFL teams that can actually win a Super Bowl is fewer than most think because "a lot of them have trouble getting out of their own way."

When Payton, who coached the New Orleans Saints from 2006 to 2021, looked to return to coaching in 2023, he searched for franchises that had a "triangle" for success. That involves ownership that provides and understands the resources and infrastructure it takes to win; a personnel department capable of finding the right players; and a coaching staff with the game-day chops and developmental skills to make the most of that talent. And all three of those sides of the triangle must be connected, with a clear vision.

"It's still finding the right people, ownership like we have in Greg and Carrie [Penner] and our group, like [general manager] George [Paton] and our relationship," Payton said. "... So when you get that triangle, and you get the ownership triangle ... you have a chance to then do the right things, a chance to acquire the right people."

Gary Kubiak, who coached the Super Bowl 50 winner and spent more than two decades with the Broncos as a player, assistant coach and head coach, had a similar mindset to Payton. He described the 2015 dynamic, when he and then-executive vice president of football operations John Elway worked together to form the roster, as a "talent puzzle."

They agreed that not all players will fit together, no matter their talent level, if there is not a clear mission about which players are acquired and retained. Talib calls it the process of finding players with "good ego" and avoiding those with "bad ego."

"Good ego is you know what you can do ... and we hold up each other to the standard, don't pull down, pull up, no grudges, just real talk," he said. "But you get bad ego, and talent don't mean s---."

Many players on both 2015 and 2026 versions of the Broncos say it's that mix that separates them. That the character and accountability have to hold up under stress and the inevitable tests of a season.

Kubiak said the current Broncos show the mission he saw in the 2015 team.

"It's always about the players,'' Kubiak said. "But the 53 most talented guys just put into the meeting room probably won't win if they don't go together. They have to demand of each other to prepare right, demand of each other to be smart, if that's something you're getting from your group, not coaches, the group, that's special."

Payton calls it the "debrief," when the game that has just been played is put through the grinder. He has often said the debrief might be more important than the game itself. No matter the result, Broncos players know what's coming.

"Honest talk," Broncos cornerback Jahdae Barron said. "Look at it, assess it, fix it. And that's everybody."

Talib, Chris Harris Jr. and T.J. Ward -- members of the 2015 secondary -- said weekly players-only film sessions by the defensive backs were a constant exercise in accountability 11 years back.

"All those cliches and s---, it's true; you don't have that 'everyone is accountable' mentality, you ain't going to get the ultimate prize," Kubiak said. "You've got to have it from the top down in the building, at every locker in your locker room."

'Just play badass defense'
The 2015 Broncos had one of the best defensive postseason runs in the Super Bowl era. Denver's defense surrendered only one total touchdown pass in three playoff games combined against Ben Roethlisberger, Tom Brady and Cam Newton, that season's MVP. The Broncos had 14 sacks and 32 quarterback hits in the playoffs, and Miller capped off that run as the ninth (and most recent) defensive player to be named Super Bowl MVP.

It was the continuation of a regular season in which the Broncos led the league in defensive EPA (by a whopping 17 points), sacks, total defense and pass defense. Denver was also No. 4 in scoring defense. The rugged, make-things-happen group allowed the 2015 team to stay afloat despite injuries and inconsistency from quarterback Peyton Manning. Manning missed seven games with a foot injury and completed a league-low 59.8% of his passes with 17 interceptions (second most in the NFL).

"We just felt, and I think as a coach you take it with you into every game, that our defense was going to keep us in it," Kubiak said. "... Even after Peyton was injured and Brock [Osweiler] was playing, we could put things together week-to-week knowing we could play tight games ... and feel good about winning them."

The current Broncos have also been led by their defense. Denver's defense led the league in sacks in each of the past two years, setting franchise records in each of those seasons. Edge rusher Nik Bonitto has turned into an All-Pro (14 sacks in 2025), finishing second to Micah Parsons last season in pressure rate among rushers with at least 300 rush attempts. Allen led all players in quarterback hits a year ago, while All-Pro cornerback Pat Surtain II (the 2024 Defensive Player of the Year) leads a deep and schematically flexible secondary.

Over the past two seasons combined, the Broncos have allowed the fewest points per game in the NFL (18.3) and have given up the lowest QBR (49.5). They have also led the league in sacks per dropback (9.4%), defensive EPA and red zone defense (opponents scored TDs on only 44.8% of drives).

"We want more, we want to get stops, we want to get the ball back for our offense, we want to keep people out of the end zone," Bonitto said. "And we all should feel like we can be better than last year just like we thought we could be better last year than we were the year before."

The Broncos finished 12th in takeaways last season, one area where they want to see improvement, but not at the expense of what defensive coordinator Vance Joseph calls "good defense." He has said that tackles need to be made with the intent to knock the ball out and interceptions need to be caught, but those aspects are not as important as third-down defense "or stopping the run or playing tough in the red zone." Better ball luck would help, too.

"I know I dropped enough that if I just catch the ones I had, the numbers look different," Broncos All-Pro safety Talanoa Hufanga said.

Count Talib as someone who is convinced the Broncos still have the defensive profile to win a Lombardi Trophy.

"[Joseph] has been cooking," Talib said. "Cooking like [former Broncos defensive coordinator Wade Phillips] was cooking with us. But VJ's matching up zones, great blitzes. VJ sees the field, he sees the game.

"It's what you need, just play badass defense. We did, they do. That gives you that edge, you put a defense with [third-year quarterback] Bo [Nix], that's everything."

'Be hard to kill'
Allen cites performance in a game's biggest moments as one of the prime indicators of a team's culture. Both the 2015 and 2025 Broncos flourished in late-game situations, with the 2015 squad going 9-3 in one-score games and last year's unit setting an NFL record with 11 one-score wins.

While close-game success can be fleeting year to year, Payton has often said the "right choices in talent acquisition" can make that performance more consistent, that confidence and belief in these moments come from "demonstrated ability."

Several 2015 Broncos players and coaches say their championship run got a nudge in Week 2 that season. In the closing seconds of regulation in Arrowhead Stadium, the Broncos were tied 24-24 with the Chiefs, who seemed content to get to overtime. But Broncos linebacker Brandon Marshall knocked the ball out of Kansas City running back Jamaal Charles' hands, and cornerback Bradley Roby scooped up the fumble and returned it for the winning touchdown with 27 seconds left.

"After that, we had a bunch of games, we made plays right at the end," Miller said. "Last seconds, a touchdown on offense, field goal, forced fumble, a sack on defense. We just felt like it would happen and it did."

The Broncos had five more wins that season in the final two minutes or in overtime, highlighted by a 48-yard touchdown run by running back C.J. Anderson in an OT win over the Patriots that ultimately decided home-field advantage in the AFC. It's a skill the current Broncos demonstrated last season and believe they have the mindset to repeat, especially as Nix has quickly become one of the NFL's preeminent "tight game" artists.

Since the start of the 2024 season, Nix is tied for the league lead with eight fourth-quarter comebacks, with five coming last season. He also led the Broncos to the winning overtime drive in the divisional round against the Buffalo Bills. And every Nix game-winning drive inspires the defense to keep games in range that much more.

"It's more about knowing, in those situations, you're going to do the right things to give you the chance,'' Allen said. "Being in the huddle knowing you've done it before and that you have the guys to do it again because everyone looking back at you wants to win more than anything else."

Denver will try to play fewer tense games while jump-starting an offense which finished tied for 13th in scoring last season and 14th in offensive EPA with two significant offseason moves. The Broncos traded for wide receiver Jaylen Waddle, and Payton relinquished primary playcalling duties to newly promoted offensive coordinator Davis Webb.

But when the stakes are high, the Broncos are confident they'll prevail. Or, as cornerback Riley Moss phrases it, they'll "just be hard to kill.''

That mindset helped the 2015 Broncos win the franchise's third Super Bowl. And Talib hopes that these Broncos can turn all that accountability, talent and big-moment success into their own Super Bowl rings.

"Of course we all want success, but you can't gatekeep s---, don't gatekeep information, don't keep secrets," Talib said. "We kept it right with each other, everybody's success is the real success.

"They play good ball, so you know they have the people who keep it right."

stories.headline: Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola calls for help from forwards: 'Need to recover the ball as high as possible'
stories.summary: Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola has called for his forward line to provide more support for the players behind them amid criticism of his team's midfield.
stories.body:
Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola has called for his forward line to provide more support for the players behind them amid criticism of his team's midfield.

Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch were both singled out for their lacklustre performances in Saturday's 0-0 draw with Fulham, with the pair combining to win just three of their 14 duels at Anfield.

However, Iraola has suggested it is not just the job of his midfield players to ensure the team is competing effectively.

"We need to recover the ball as high as possible because it makes the offensive side that much easier," the Liverpool boss said. "We have situations to attack in one v one.

"It's more than the midfield. When we have been good collectively the midfielders have looked a lot better and recovered more balls. We are helping them more to win the duels. The ones up front do their job very well then the midfielders look good.

"If we are allowing them to defend one v one all the time and we are not aggressive, then also our defenders will struggle.

"If the players ahead of you are doing the job then midfielders look better. It is more collective. That's the help we have to give to our defenders and midfielders so everyone looks better, looks smarter and in better positions."

- Andoni Iraola cites 'lack of freshness' after Liverpool's draw with Fulham

- Liverpool ratings: Barcola, Wirtz, Gravenberch struggle at Anfield

Liverpool will look to bounce back from the weekend's disappointment when they host Tottenham Hotspur in the third round of the Carabao Cup on Tuesday night.

It will be the Reds' third game in seven days, with Iraola confirming he is set to use his full squad against Roberto De Zerbi's side.

"I'm very happy with the squad," he said.

"I value a lot the players we have. If we win games the squad looks fantastic, if we don't win then there are problems or whatever. We will see tomorrow players we haven't seen and I am looking forward to seeing them. They can help us and they haven't had the chance yet."

stories.headline: MLB 2026: Yordan Alvarez's Triple Crown, MVP potential
stories.summary: History or not, Alvarez's offensive campaign stands alone. Here's his status in the MVP race, how his season would rank among Triple Crown winners and more.
stories.body:
Baseball's Triple Crown -- when a player finishes the season leading their league in the three major statistical categories -- is one of the most difficult achievements in sports, with Miguel Cabrera in 2012 the only hitter to lead in batting average, home runs and RBIs since 1967.

And for a majority of MLB's 2026 regular season, Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez had been on a historic path to join Cabrera.

On Aug. 2, he went 4-for-5 with three doubles and two RBIs, lifting his season average to .330 to lead the American League batting title race by an astounding 29 points over Tampa Bay's Yandy Diaz (the only other AL player even hitting .300) while also topping the circuit with 35 home runs (four more than New York's Ben Rice) and 84 RBIs (11 more than Rice).

The 16th Triple Crown season since 1900 was not just in play for Alvarez -- it felt almost inevitable on that day. He not only towered over his fellow AL batsmen, but those from the National League as well: His 1.092 OPS was 145 points higher than Juan Soto's NL-leading mark. This was Alvarez, one of the major leagues' best hitters since his debut in 2019, at his most fearsome and his best, healthy and locked in.

But from that high-water mark, Alvarez has slowed down: Since Aug. 2, he has hit .242/.380/.383 with only three home runs and 12 RBIs in 35 games. His lead in the batting race has dwindled to five points over Tampa Bay's Chandler Simpson, and he now trails Simpson's teammate, Junior Caminero, in home runs (40-38) and Baltimore's Pete Alonso in RBIs (100-96).

Though there's still time for Alvarez to regain those leads, he'll have to heat up over these final two weeks. Nonetheless, it's still an astonishing season. His OPS remains over 1.000 at 1.016, while Willson Contreras ranks second in the AL hovering around the .900 mark. The last time a player led his league with an OPS over 1.000 and no other hitter was over .900 was 1946, when Stan Musial posted a 1.021 OPS to lead the NL with Whitey Kurowski second at .853.

Let's dive into Alvarez's 2026 campaign by taking a look at his current positioning in the MVP race, as well as where his season would potentially rank among Triple Crown winners if he's able to finish strong in September and secure the honor.

Where Alvarez stands in the AL MVP race

Alvarez's fade over the past month has perhaps opened up the AL MVP race. But recent MVP votes have tended to go one way, with last year's Aaron Judge-Cal Raleigh debate the rare example of a reasonably close vote. All four of Shohei Ohtani's MVP selections have been unanimous, as was Judge's win in 2024 and Ronald Acuna Jr.'s in 2023 (even though Mookie Betts had a slight edge in Baseball-Reference WAR). Judge outscored Ohtani 28-2 in 2022, even though both had amazing seasons. The last time more than two players received a first-place vote was in the NL in 2022, when Paul Goldschmidt got 22 votes, Manny Machado seven and Nolan Arenado one.

It's possible this year's AL vote ends up resembling the 2021 NL vote, when Bryce Harper won with 17 first-place votes while four different players -- each with a higher bWAR than Harper -- also received first-place votes. Harper led in OPS and Soto led in WAR, while the more well-rounded trio of Fernando Tatis Jr., Brandon Crawford and Trea Turner finished third, fourth and fifth, respectively.

The MVP narrative in 2026 has certainly swung in Alvarez's direction since midsummer, but he currently ranks third in combo WAR (the average of Baseball-Reference and FanGraphs) entering Sunday. Let's consider the other top MVP candidates:

1. Bobby Witt Jr., Kansas City Royals: 6.4 (combo WAR)

The problem with Witt's case: A lot of his value comes from his Gold Glove defense -- not to mention the MVP vote typically favors the best offensive players, as was the case with Harper -- plus the Royals are mired in last place. Though playing for a playoff-bound team is no longer a requirement as it once was (Harper's Phillies didn't reach the postseason in 2021), Witt doesn't even rank in the top 10 in the AL in OPS and has driven in only 54 runs. He might get a few first-place votes as the best all-around player in the league, but it's hard to envision a player on a last-place team who might barely get to 60 RBIs winning MVP honors.

2. Cam Schlittler, New York Yankees: 6.2

Schlittler leads the AL in bWAR and is 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA and 228 strikeouts following another dominant start Sunday (one hit in six scoreless innings). He has been the key player on a team that struggled to score runs with Judge sidelined for 100 days -- and Schlittler has been big down the stretch, with seven straight starts giving up one run or no runs.

The problem: Pitchers don't win MVP awards. Well, not in the past decade anyway. Clayton Kershaw won in 2014, when he went 21-3 with a 1.77 ERA and 8.2 WAR, and Justin Verlander won in 2011, when he went 24-5 with a 2.40 ERA and 8.6 WAR, but Schlittler won't come close to 20 wins like those two. The only full-time pitchers this decade to finish in the top five of the voting were Shane Bieber (fourth in 2020) and Tarik Skubal (fifth in 2025).

3. Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros: 5.8

Alvarez has played 23 games in the outfield, but he's primarily a DH. Ohtani became the first DH to win MVP in 2024 (the year he didn't pitch), so the DH stigma is no longer a barrier as it might have been for Edgar Martinez in 1995 or David Ortiz a couple of times (including his final season in 2016, when he was the best hitter in the AL but finished sixth in the MVP vote). Ohtani, however, posted 9.0 WAR in his 50/50 season, a total Alvarez won't come close to reaching. Still, Alvarez is the best hitter in a soft MVP race, and though his WAR would be one of the lowest ever for an MVP winner, he's the favorite -- especially if the Astros hold on to their AL West lead.

4. Dylan Cease, Toronto Blue Jays: 5.7

Fantastic season, but he's behind Schlittler as far as pitchers go.

5. Kevin McGonigle, Detroit Tigers: 5.6

Like Witt, McGonigle has had an excellent all-around season thanks to good defense and a high OBP, but he'll have to settle for Rookie of the Year.

6. Junior Caminero, Tampa Bay Rays: 5.2

He's sixth in combo WAR, but he's the player most likely to challenge Alvarez for MVP honors. Caminero is close in bWAR, 5.4 to Alvarez's 5.8, and could actually end up winning two of the three Triple Crown categories, since he leads in home runs and is third in RBIs, five behind Alonso and one behind Alvarez. Caminero's defensive metrics hold down his WAR, especially on FanGraphs, but if the Rays do win the AL East, he will get a lot of credit for that.

His hopes might rest on two things: delivering a strong final two weeks and the Texas Rangers running down the Astros in the AL West, with Alvarez continuing to slump.

If Alvarez does reclaim his Triple Crown leads, where would his season rank?

The impact of his WAR on the MVP race will be moot if Alvarez reclaims his Triple Crown leads.

That is what propelled Cabrera to the 2012 AL MVP Award over rookie Mike Trout, even though Trout had a huge edge in WAR, 10.5 to 7.1. Indeed, the vote wasn't even close, with Cabrera collecting 22 of the 28 first-place votes. He'd been the first Triple Crown winner in 45 years, since Carl Yastrzemski in 1967, and many voters were just learning about the WAR metric for the first time. In Cabrera's case, the Triple Crown narrative and old-school numbers beat out Trout's own rookie sensation narrative and new-school analytics.

Cabrera's Triple Crown shows how difficult it is to line up all three categories in the same season. Judge has twice led in home runs and RBIs in seasons he hit .311 and .322 but didn't win batting titles. He won the AL batting title last year with a .331 mark, but Seattle's Raleigh topped him in home runs and RBIs with his own historic season. Cabrera himself had better seasons than his 2012 campaign, but the stars aligned that year: He topped Curtis Granderson and Josh Hamilton by one home run, had an 11-RBI edge over Hamilton and beat out Trout by four points for the batting title.

But among the 15 Triple Crown winners, Cabrera's 168 OPS+ ranks last and his .999 OPS beats out only dead-ball winners Heinie Zimmerman and Ty Cobb. Alvarez's current OPS+ of 185 would also rank near the bottom of Triple Crown winners:

Ted Williams, 1942 AL: 216

Mickey Mantle, 1956 AL: 210

Rogers Hornsby, 1925 NL: 210

Lou Gehrig, 1934 AL: 207

Rogers Hornsby, 1922 NL: 207

Ted Williams, 1947 AL: 205

Jimmie Foxx, 1933 AL: 201

Frank Robinson, 1966 AL: 198

Nap Lajoie, 1901 AL: 198

Carl Yastrzemski, 1967 AL: 193

Ty Cobb, 1909 AL: 192

Yordan Alvarez, 2026 AL: 185

Joe Medwick, 1937 NL: 182

Chuck Klein, 1933 NL: 176

Heinie Zimmerman, 1912 NL: 170

Miguel Cabrera, 2012 AL: 168

Another way to measure dominance is the edge the Triple Crown winner had over the No. 2 players in each category. Mantle hit 52 home runs in 1956, a remarkable 20-homer margin over Vic Wertz, although his leads in the other two categories were smaller.

Williams had significant margins in all three categories in 1942: nine home runs, 23 RBIs and 25 points in batting average. He finished second in the MVP voting that year to Joe Gordon of the Yankees, who won the pennant. When Williams won his second Triple Crown in 1947, he again finished second in the MVP voting, this time to Joe DiMaggio of the -- yes -- first-place Yankees. Williams hit .343-32-114 (with a .499 OBP) while DiMaggio hit .315-20-97 (with a .391 OBP). Don't even ask about the then-non-existent WAR: Williams led 9.5 to 4.7. In those days, the MVP winner almost always went to a pennant-winning player.

Frank Robinson's Triple Crown in 1966 -- which came after the Reds traded him to the Orioles -- was impressive as well and flies under the radar among great offensive seasons. He hit 49 home runs, 10 more than Harmon Killebrew, and had leads of 12 RBIs and nine batting-average points. Robinson created an estimated 146 runs, in a league in which only four other players topped 100. He had a 118-point lead in OPS over Killebrew.

The most impressive Triple Crown season, however, might belong to Hornsby -- it's just a matter of which one. Let's go with 1922. Check out his totals and lead over the No. 2 guy in each category:

42 HRs: 16 over Cy Williams (the only other player with more than 20)
152 RBIs: 20 over Irish Meusel (and the No. 3 guy was 40 behind)
.401 AVG: 47 points over Ray Grimes
1.181 OPS: 167 points over Grimes (and 269 points over the No. 3 guy)
202 runs created: 75 over Max Carey (that might be the largest margin ever. Barry Bonds never had a lead that big, and Babe Ruth had a 70-run edge in his career-best season in 1921)

Jimmie Foxx's 1933 Triple Crown campaign -- .356-48-163 -- is also in the discussion for best ever, with leads of 20 points in average, 14 in home runs and 23 in RBIs. His season is extra impressive since it came in a league with Lou Gehrig, Babe Ruth, Charlie Gehringer, Al Simmons and other Hall of Famers (eight of the top 10 players in batting average, for example, are Hall of Famers).

Still, I'll go with Hornsby's 1922 as the best Triple Crown season, edging out Williams' 1942 and Foxx's 1933.

Alvarez, if he finishes strong and makes history, won't be on that level, but it will go down as an offensive season to remember. The Triple Crown would speak for itself, but the context of baseball in 2026 must be considered: Nobody in the AL is close to Alvarez. Entering Sunday, he had created 138 runs -- 35 more than Caminero and Alonso. That would be the seventh-biggest differential over the No. 2 guy among Triple Crown winners. Pete Crow-Armstrong is close in the NL and he's second in the majors in OPS -- a distant 81 points behind Alvarez.

In a season in which pitching has dominated and few hitters have put up monster numbers, Alvarez stands alone. Triple Crown or not.

stories.headline: Philadelphia 76ers offseason recap, early 2026-27 season preview
stories.summary: The Sixers overhauled their front office and their roster this offseason. Will the major moves end Philly's title drought?
stories.body:
The Philadelphia 76ers opened the offseason with a shocking trade on July 1, sending Paul George, two first-round picks (2028, 2031) and two second-round selections (2028, 2030) to the Boston Celtics in exchange for Finals MVP Jaylen Brown. Brown had been rumored in Giannis Antetokounmpo trade packages before the former Milwaukee Bucks star ended up in Miami.

Before July came to a close, the Sixers made waves again, this time landing the biggest free agent of the offseason in LeBron James. The 41-year-old agreed to extremely team-friendly terms with the Sixers, inking a two-year, $8 million deal (he made nearly $53 million last season with the Los Angeles Lakers).

The offseason moves come after the Sixers parted ways with former general manager Daryl Morey after six seasons in May before promoting assistant general manager Jameer Nelson to be the team's executive vice president of basketball operations under new president Mike Gansey.

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Friday. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for all 30 teams.

Let's dive into the Sixers, who are hopeful their offseason splashes catapult them to the top of the East:

Quick links:

Roster | Depth chart | Transactions

More Sixers coverage | More NBA

Offseason at a glance
Key additions: F LeBron James, G Jaylen Brown, G Anfernee Simons, F Dean Wade, G Labaron Philon Jr., G Kentavious Caldwell-Pope

Key subtractions: F Paul George, C Andre Drummond, G Quentin Grimes, G Kelly Oubre Jr.

No team changed its fortunes from April to July as drastically as the 76ers. Taking advantage of Boston's desire to get out of the Jaylen Brown business enabled it to accomplish so much: getting a motivated All-Star feeling the sting of rejection following a career year, dumping George's contract and putting themselves in position to be attractive to an all-time great in James, who was looking for a new challenge. They also lessened their dependency on Joel Embiid's bothersome health as he will turn 33 during the season.

They filled in the blanks by adding Caldwell-Pope and Wade as plug-and-play wings, changing the complexion of their franchise in several swoops. If nothing else, they won the offseason. -- Vincent Goodwill

Zach Kram's offseason grade: A-

Regardless of Brown's precise value, turning 36-year-old George into a 29-year-old All-NBA wing is a big win for Philadelphia. The forward positions have long been a concern for the 76ers, but they're on much firmer ground now with Brown and Wade, and Brown is specifically a strong fit next to Embiid because of his reliability.

The 76ers' roster isn't perfect -- it lacks some shooting and is still too reliant on Embiid for its size -- but Philadelphia at least has a narrow path to the Finals now, when such a route didn't exist before this summer. -- Kram

What we learned over the past few months
From Ben Golliver's offseason lessons piece: The 76ers aren't Embiid's team anymore.

Philadelphia's new front office executed one of the biggest moves of the summer when it traded George and draft picks to acquire Brown from the Boston Celtics. The move made sense on many levels: Brown is younger, healthier and more productive than George.

However, Brown's arrival introduces some new questions related to the Sixers' franchise center. Brown and Embiid are both high-usage scorers who like to operate in the midrange and get to the free throw line. By comparison, George was a more natural complement to Embiid; he's a better 3-point shooter and proved willing to sacrifice shots during his Philadelphia tenure.

Brown and Embiid could probably strike a "two alphas" balance if they were surrounded by role players, but Philadelphia's loaded backcourt includes All-Star Tyrese Maxey and rising star VJ Edgecombe. There's a lot of scoring talent on hand, and something will have to give.

Embiid has appeared in just 39% of games over the past three seasons, and he missed four of the 76ers' 11 playoff games last season. While Embiid is Philadelphia's oldest player at 32, Brown, Maxey, Edgecombe and summer additions Wade, Simons and Philon are all in their 20s.

Put all those factors together, and Brown seemingly makes more sense for Philadelphia's post-Embiid future than he does as an Embiid sidekick. The next question: When would a transition take place given that Embiid still has three years remaining on his contract? -- Golliver

The big question: Can the 76ers come together to be a contender by the playoffs?
Embiid's health will be monitored, as it has been the past few years. So will James', as he's averaged an admirable 67 games the past three years as he plays well into his 40s. Much regular-season weight will be placed on a new acquisition in Brown, a second-year emerging star in Edgecombe and a franchise mainstay in Maxey.

Will there be enough continuity through the first six months to cash in during the playoffs? Recent history says it takes a couple of years for talent to coalesce, but do the 76ers have that kind of time with James and Embiid? James' personal history says by Year 2, his teams are ready to win titles. It seems, though, that the 76ers are loaded up for this June, not next June. -- Goodwill

NBA trade grades: Why the Sixers get an A+ in the LeBron deal

Basketball Power Index rank: No. 6
Here are the predicted Net Points per 100 possessions for the 76ers' top seven players for the 2026-27 season:

James has been part of 15 of the 39 teams with the highest combined career usages of their top five players. This includes seasons with Dwayne Wade, Luka Doncic, Kyrie Irving, Russell Westbrook, Kevin Love, Carmelo Anthony, Anthony Davis, Ray Allen and Chris Bosh. The average record of those teams was 52-30, which is basically what this team is predicted to do.

For the haters, the worst of those 15 teams was the 33-win Lakers team in 2021-22 with Russ, Melo and AD. The preseason over/under for wins for that team was, per Basketball-Reference, also 52 games. -- Dean Oliver

Read about how Net Points works here.

Windy: Why LeBron chose the Sixers over the Cavs, Heat
NBA coaches, execs react to LeBron signing
Inside LeBron's decision to join the Sixers

Biggest X factor this season
Centers Adem Bona and Ariel Hukporti

Embiid has missed more than half of the past three regular seasons, so even if he turns in a relatively healthy season, his backups will still get plenty of work. Bona and Hukporti will therefore be tasked with both keeping the 76ers afloat when Embiid is absent (so the 76ers don't fall behind in a very competitive Eastern Conference playoff race) and helping the 2023 MVP reach the playoffs healthy.

It's an odd thing to say about a team with such star power in the starting lineup, but their ultimate outcome this season could also hinge on two unheralded backup centers. -- Kram

Betting insight from our expert
Bet to make ahead of the season: To reach conference semifinals (-125); to make conference finals (+200)

The 76ers reached the conference semifinals last season after winning their play-in game and then upsetting the No. 2 seed Celtics in the first round. They then proceeded to make the biggest splash in the NBA this offseason, bringing in former Finals MVPs Brown and James to supplement their core of Maxey, Embiid and Edgecombe.

While changes this big could lead to some growing pains, and both former MVPs (James and Embiid) have age and injury concerns, the talent on this team suggests they could contend for the NBA title. Getting essentially even money for the team to just get as far as they made it last season feels like solid value. -- Andre Snellings

stories.headline: Spanish GP takeaways: Kimi Antonelli marches on as Lando Norris suffers, Madring falls flat
stories.summary: The Spanish Grand Prix is done and dusted and drivers got their first taste of the brand-new Madring.
stories.body:
MADRID, Spain -- The Spanish Grand Prix is done and dusted and drivers got their first taste of the brand-new Madring.

Teams, drivers and fans were predicting chaos with safety cars and red flags, but it ended up being one of the less dramatic races on the calendar.

Here are the biggest takeaways from the last European race of the season.

- Spanish Grand Prix: Kimi Antonelli wins again as Lando Norris rues bad luck, Lewis Hamilton suffers DNF

- Lando Norris hits out at F1 Virtual Safety Car rule after losing 'deserved' Spanish GP win

- Madring's F1 debut left everyone dissatisfied, even Spanish GP's top 3

No one can stop Kimi Antonelli
Kimi Antonelli has been by far and away the dominant force of the 2026 season, and the Spanish Grand Prix provided another example of why he is becoming so difficult to stop.

Sometimes Antonelli has simply been the fastest driver. Other times, fortune has fallen his way. In Spain, it was a bit of both.

The 20-year-old looked like the man to beat for much of qualifying, putting his Mercedes on provisional pole before Lando Norris stole it from him late on. Norris appeared to have the upper hand again in the race, only for the Virtual Safety Car to give Mercedes the opportunity to pit Antonelli immediately and switch onto hard tyres to run the finish.

Antonelli admitted afterwards that "Lando deserved the win," but there is something increasingly ominous about the way this championship is unfolding. When Antonelli has the quickest car, he wins. And when he doesn't, he keeps putting himself in a position to capitalise when something goes wrong for his rivals.

It is not the first time this season that circumstances have played into his hands, but Antonelli has been virtually faultless in taking advantage of them. It's no wonder Lewis Hamilton said: "There's no stopping him and Mercedes this year."

At this rate, the question is becoming less about whether Antonelli can become Formula 1's youngest world champion and more about what, or who, can possibly stop him.

Norris left wondering what might have been
The reigning world champion has been on fire in the last few races. He took back-to-back wins in Hungary and Zandvoort and has squeezed everything out of McLaren's upgrade package, introduced before Hungary.

He arrived in Madrid as F1's form driver and left wondering how a weekend in which he did so much right ended without another victory.

Norris came from nowhere and managed to find over seven-tenths on his final lap to stun Antonelli to the line in qualifying with what he described as "one of the best laps" of his career.

But if Antonelli has had a habit of being in the right place at the right time this season, Norris experienced the opposite in Madrid.

He passed the pit entry at the same time the VSC was being deployed, and because he had enough of an advantage out in front, his rivals were able to benefit. Antonelli and Max Verstappen were two of many to come in -- saving 11 seconds in the process under the slower conditions. His misfortune was compounded when the VSC ended just before he completed the next lap. Norris pitted anyway, but the damage was done. He emerged 15 seconds behind Antonelli, and more than nine behind Verstappen.

Should the rule change, as Norris has suggested? It could create more problems than answers. Either way, it was a cruel end to a weekend in which Norris had again shown why he is becoming an increasing threat to Mercedes. He may not have got the result to show for it, but his pace -- and that of the upgraded McLaren -- suggests there will be more opportunities to come.

Madrid has an overtaking problem
The highly anticipated newly-branded Spanish GP was a race everyone was curious about as teams and drivers had no historic data available to help them build strategies and predict performances heading into the weekend.

Drivers described the track as one of the most "challenging" on the calendar and a "car-killer," and after several crashes in both F2 and F3, everyone was strapping in for a chaotic race.

It ended up being a fairly stagnant race with not much movement in the top five, and despite a battle unfolding between Norris and Verstappen for second over the final 10 laps, nothing ended up materialising.

Part of the problem was the lack of overtaking opportunities.

Several circuits on the calendar have tight, heavy-braking corners which are attached to long straights, providing the perfect opportunity for overtaking.

But at the Madring, there were no slow-speed corners to get any kind of move done. The main opportunity to overtake was Turn 5, but that didn't provide much action.

The feeling in the paddock is that F1 perhaps needs to come up with modifications for future races to allow overtaking to happen, which could then lead to a more exciting race.

Race winner Antonelli said: "It definitely doesn't create overtaking opportunities and it doesn't push you to try and make a move because 80% of the time you might have a contact."

Haas driver Oliver Bearman added: "It's been a bit of a disappointment, but hopefully next year it will be a bit more interesting. When you arrive and you see that layout and you are like, 'what do you expect us to do', it's a bit disappointing ... Basically from Turn 5, all the way from 17, there was a bit of free reign, let's say. I don't think that free reign was used to the best of its potential."

"I think what F1, we'd like to review, is that there's some modifications required at the circuit in order to introduce an overtaking possibility," McLaren team principal Andrea Stella added.

"Because at the moment, the fact is that the straight may be long enough, but there's absolutely no way the two cars can enter the corner fine together. So, let's say, it's basically impossible an attempt of overtaking."

Championship running away from Hamilton
It was another heartbreaking weekend for Lewis Hamilton after he retired from the Spanish Grand Prix.

The Ferrari driver celebrated a historic first victory for the team at the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix in June, and it would have been fitting to add another win to his tally while racing in Spain.

But he suffered a brake issue on the very first lap and while the team tried to find a solution the issue from the pit wall, nobody could help him.

Hamilton's DNF, his first mechanical failure at Ferrari, puts him 101 points behind race winner Antonelli.

Before the summer break, the seven-time world champion was very much in the title fight and was only 32 points adrift from Antonelli at the start of July.

But as the season unravels, it is looking like that incredible title race that could have been, has perhaps been lost.

stories.headline: How Team USA rallied to beat France and win World Cup gold
stories.summary: France led by 14 points early, but the U.S. defense dominated and veterans stepped up to capture a fifth straight gold.
stories.body:
The U.S. women's basketball team has not lost a game in major international play since 2006 and has lost only one gold medal game (in 1983). Yet when the Americans faced a double-digit deficit in the first half of the FIBA Women's World Cup final Sunday, they couldn't just rely on history.

They had to get it done on court.

Team USA beat France 97-79 in Berlin to win its fifth consecutive World Cup title and 12th overall. Trailing 45-43 at halftime, the Americans took control in the third quarter, outscoring France 30-12. That dominance decided the game and the gold medal.

Coming in, France had been the more impressive team in the tournament, winning its five games by an average of 35.6 points with no margin closer than 22. Team USA, by contrast, beat Italy in group play by three points and Spain in the semifinals by 10. A strong start Sunday kept the momentum on France's side.

But then the U.S. defense took it up a notch in the second half, and the offense followed. The mojo changed entirely in the Americans' favor, with multiple players stepping forward.

Stars such as four-time WNBA MVP A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum were out due to injuries. That led to seven of the 12 U.S. players competing in their first major 5-on-5 international competition, including Rhyne Howard, Aliyah Boston, Caitlin Clark and Paige Bueckers, the past four WNBA Rookie of the Year award winners.

But the veterans supplemented all the "new," led by Jackie Young, Breanna Stewart, Chelsea Gray, Kahleah Copper and Napheesa Collier. Young, who had 18 points, six rebounds and five assists, was Sunday's player of the game. Stewart, who had 22 points, 10 rebounds and four assists, was MVP of the tournament.

Now the WNBA players from all the teams in this tournament head back to finish the regular season and get ready for the playoffs. But here's how Team USA stayed on top of the world and denied France its first World Cup gold.

How did Team USA go from trailing by 14 points to winning by 18?

Voepel: Defense. France was getting the shots it wanted and making them in the first half. That had been the case throughout this tournament, as the French offense had controlled all its previous games.

That changed in the second half, as the U.S. women relied on both their individual defensive strengths and their ability to switch without losing anything in their matchups. Everything the Americans did in the third quarter defensively was sharper, quicker and more focused. Not surprisingly, forcing France into missed shots and turnovers fueled the Americans' offense.

U.S. coach Kara Lawson is known as a defensive coach at Duke, and U.S. assistant Natalie Nakase guides the WNBA's top defensive team, the Golden State Valkyries. That expertise on the bench and the defensive strengths of the Americans' veterans turned around the game.

Stewart told TNT after the game that even when the Americans were down 14, they really weren't rattled. The fact that they cut the deficit to two by halftime -- a big steal by Angel Reese led to a 3-pointer by Clark before the buzzer -- gave the team a boost. And the Americans looked very confident starting the third quarter. Those 10 minutes made all the difference.

Philippou: Lawson said the second quarter might have been her favorite of the game. The U.S. women still trailed by two when the period ended, but the momentum had shifted in their favor -- especially after those plays from Reese and Clark -- and they had started to figure out some things. Once they got into the locker room, they could home in on how to fix the defensive lapses that plagued them early on.

At halftime, Stewart said, Lawson told the players that France might stay with them for three quarters, but by the time they got to the fourth, the United States was going to be able to bust things open. "Little do we know," Stewart said, "it came in the third quarter."

And before long, Team USA looked to have regained the psychological edge, getting whatever it wanted on both ends. Another back-breaking moment was when France got called for two flagrants in a single play at the end of the third quarter, which resulted in a five-point possession for the United States and extended its lead to 73-57 going into the fourth.

"We have to give France a lot of credit," Clark said. "They play with a lot of grit. They play with a lot of passion. They're aggressive. But I think we showed what wearing a USA jersey is all about. It's about dominating, and that's exactly what we did."

Did it hurt that France wasn't tested until the gold medal game?

Voepel: This wasn't a tight game down to the wire in which France might have needed that experience. However, where it perhaps cost the French is that they hadn't faced a defense as good as what Team USA threw at them in the third quarter. France had been especially good all tournament from behind the arc, and it again reached double-digit 3-pointers with 11 on Sunday. But the French went from 8-of-14 from 3-point range in the first half to 3-of-10 in the second.

And Gabby Williams, who had been a force all tournament, went from 16 points in the first half to four in the second. Marine Johannes, one of France's main sharpshooters, had just one 3-pointer in the game.

How well did Team USA's newcomers play?

Voepel: Overall, they did their jobs, and that says a lot when you add in the extra pressure of playing for your country. Tons of eyes were on Clark, of course, and she had a double-double in Team USA's opener vs. China. While she didn't shoot as well from 3-point range as she would have liked during the tournament (7-for-25, 28%), she was 2-of-3 from behind the arc Sunday and 4-of-5 from the field. She finished with 12 points and three assists and led Team USA in overall assists for the tournament with 32. Reese also made her presence felt, especially on the defensive end of the court where her size and quick hands flustered foes.

Guards Clark and Bueckers don't have anywhere near as much experience at the international level or in playing together as Gray and Young, who have been Las Vegas Aces teammates for six years with three WNBA titles. That helps explain why Lawson relied more on the vets during the most stressful periods in the Americans' close games but gave the youngsters playing time throughout the tournament so that the vets weren't worn out by the gold medal game.

Every Team USA basketball coach -- women's and men's -- is always heavily scrutinized for how they balance having so much talent and distributing minutes. In the end, give Lawson credit for how she allowed growth and important court time for the young players but also understood when veteran experience was what Team USA needed most.

Philippou: Taking the tournament as a whole, all of the young players had some really strong moments, showed where they have some room for growth and demonstrated the promise of what they might be able to do over time as a collective. And while Lawson relied heavily on the vets against France, what those younger players absorbed from the experience of playing for the senior national team and observing the older players is invaluable. With Team USA coming home with gold and its winning streak in major international tournaments intact, it was as good of a debut as could realistically be expected.

What does this win mean for Team USA?

Voepel: It's a new era for the world's dominant power in women's basketball but the same result. Team USA's last loss in a major international competition was in the 2006 World Cup semifinals to Russia. Before that, the most recent American losses were in the 1992 Olympic semifinals to what was then called the Unified Team (essentially the former Soviet Union with an interim name) and the 1994 World Cup semifinals to Brazil.

While we already noted Team USA's only major competition loss in a gold medal game came in the 1983 World Cup to the Soviet Union, the Americans have one other silver medal. That came in the 1976 Olympics, the first time the Summer Games had women's basketball. But that was a six-team round-robin tournament that the Soviets won by going 5-0. Team USA was 3-2 but took silver thanks to its round-robin win over fellow 3-2 team Bulgaria.

All that history is important to illustrate how outstanding Team USA has been in the Olympics and World Cup and to show what an upset it would have been had France taken the gold Sunday. It would have been just the third silver for Team USA.

All these World Cup players could be back in the mix for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, along with Wilson, Plum and up-and-coming younger standouts such as WNBA rookie Olivia Miles and college stars such as JuJu Watkins, Sarah Strong and Hannah Hidalgo. The pipeline for talent continues to be full.

Philippou: And yet the tournament reminded us that winning is hard, even as USA Basketball often makes it look easy, and it's getting even more difficult as the quality of play and teams improves globally.

Sue Bird, the managing director for the U.S. women's national team, made an interesting point in a pregame news conference: With more international players coming to the WNBA and getting plenty familiar with the Americans, the psychological factor of being intimidated by Team USA on a World Cup or Olympic stage won't be as prevalent. The United States won't be able to rest on its laurels if it wants to continue its run of dominance, and it'll be interesting to see how the U.S. women continue to evolve and grow.

What does the loss mean for France?

Voepel: The French wanted this very badly and played great for 5½ games in this tournament. But the second half Sunday was like the clock striking midnight on France's hopes. The French just couldn't match Team USA when the Americans went to their next gear. That said, look at the progress France has made internationally and in the WNBA; 13 French players have been on WNBA rosters this season. The sky is the limit for a youngster like Seattle Storm center Dominique Malonga (21 points, six rebounds Sunday). France lost by just one point to the United States in the 2024 Olympic final in Paris and now takes silver in the World Cup.

Add that to Spain's bronze medal and host Germany's fourth-place finish, and it's an excellent showing for Europe, whose players have become a significantly bigger factor in helping the WNBA improve its talent level and global footprint. Plus, France and the rest of Europe will be all the more motivated for the Los Angeles Games in two years.

stories.headline: Arsenal's Gabriel 'eager' to take another Champions League final penalty: 'If it happens again, I'll be there'
stories.summary: Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhães has said that he is "eager" for another chance to take a penalty in a Champions League final.
stories.body:
Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhães has said told ESPN that he is "eager" for another chance to take a penalty in a Champions League final after the heartbreak of missing the crucial spot kick in last season's final against Paris Saint-Germain.

Following an earlier miss from Eberechi Eze in the shootout, Arsenal's hopes of winning their first European trophy rested on the shoulders of the Brazil defender who ultimately sent the ball over the crossbar to crown PSG champions for a second consecutive season.

Gabriel, a stalwart character of the Arsenal defence, told ESPN Brasil that if he was in a similar position again, he would take another penalty.

"I couldn't let a single missed penalty erase everything I'd achieved during the season," he said.

"So, I just thank God for the opportunity to have been there in that moment, it's part of the football.

"But I'm definitely eager for another chance, if it happens again, I'll be there, and if I have to take the penalty, I'll take it. So, that's it."

Arsenal were praised throughout last season's campaign for their solid defence, conceding just seven goals throughout their European campaign.

Gabriel thanked the fans for their continued support despite their European season ending on a sour note.

"I only have to thank the fans," he told ESPN Brasil. "Ever since the final, I've just received a lot of support from them, you know. They were incredible to me, sending very positive messages.

"But like I said, it's part of football. I'm here, and it's not the first time something like this has happened. So, as I said, if there's another penalty for me to take, I'll take it."

- Arsenal reach agreement to sign 17-year-old winger Andria Bartishvili

- Mikel Arteta reveals how he sabotaged Arsenal preseason to prepare for chaos

- Mikel Arteta 'surprised' by criticism over handling of Gabriel Jesus, Gabriel Martinelli exits

Despite the missed opportunity in the Champions League final, Arsenal did end their 22-year wait for the Premier League title and look as though their form is continuing on into this campaign.

Mikel Arteta's side are yet to drop points this season but face a stiff test when they take on Sunderland at the Stadium of Light on Saturday.

stories.headline: Dylan Larkin to attend Red Wings camp despite trade request
stories.summary: Longtime captain Dylan Larkin will be at Red Wings training camp despite requesting a trade this offseason. Though Larkin will be in attendance, the team said it will begin the season without a captain.
stories.body:
Longtime Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin will report to training camp in Detroit next week despite his summer trade request.

However the Red Wings announced that they will begin the season without a captain.

"Over the past couple of weeks, Red Wings leadership and I have had several in-depth discussions. I've appreciated those candid conversations, and I will be at training camp with my teammates," Larkin said in a statement. "When new leadership is in place, we'll talk further about the direction of the team. We will keep those conversations private, and I will keep my focus on the season ahead and on the guys in that room."

In July, shortly after Larkin's trade request became public, the Red Wings announced that Steve Yzerman would no longer be the team's general manager. Yzerman, a franchise legend and Hall of Famer, had been GM since 2019. Detroit entered a rebuild in that time and hasn't made the playoffs in 10 years.

In a statement, the Red Wings said they "look forward to seeing Dylan and his teammates at Little Caesars for the start of training camp," which begins Sept. 17.

"Any further discussions or decisions regarding this topic will be made once new hockey operations leadership is in place," the team said.

The Red Wings have hired a search firm, which has been conducting interviews for a new general manager.

Larkin, 30, grew up in nearby Waterford, Michigan, and played at the University of Michigan. He was selected by his hometown team in the first round of the 2014 NHL draft.

He debuted in the 2015-16 season for the Red Wings, and the team made the playoffs in his rookie season -- the final year of the franchise's NHL-record 25-year playoff streak. Detroit lost to Tampa Bay in five games in the first round and hasn't returned since.

Larkin was a key member of the 2026 U.S. men's Olympic team that won its first gold medal since 1980. He was especially important defensively and on special teams, part of a penalty killing unit that went a flawless 18-for-18 in Milan.

The Minnesota Wild -- led by Bill Guerin, also the general manager of Team USA -- have tried to acquire Larkin, according to sources. However the sides have been at a stalemate this summer, especially as Detroit's GM seat is vacant.

Larkin had been Detroit's captain since 2021. He ranks 10th in franchise history in both goals (276) and points (643).

The Red Wings' offseason has been defined by uncertainty. That led in part to the free agent departure of Patrick Kane, who returned to the Chicago Blackhawks. Another key piece of business that's unresolved: ascending star defenseman Simon Edvinsson is due for a contract extension.

stories.headline: Updated: NRL 2026 team-by-team season review
stories.summary: The 2026 NRL season proper has come to an end, so it's time to evaluate every team's year.
stories.body:
The 2026 NRL season proper has come to an end, so it's time to evaluate every team's year. We take a look back at our preseason prediction, assess the way each team travelled, and work out their grades for 2026.

This will be updated as every team's season finishes.

Brisbane Broncos
Last year's ladder finish: 4th (Premiers)

Predicted 2026 finish: 3rd

Actual finish: 14th

Grade: F

Very rarely does a premiership winning side fall so far, so quickly. Everyone fully expected that the Broncos would mount an impressive title defence on the back of what they achieved in 2025 and the relative stability of their squad. What the pundits and fans could not predict was the behind-the-scenes discourse, the injuries to key players, and the apparent complete lack of commitment from players out in the middle. The coach losing the locker room is an often-used excuse, usually followed by the sacking of the coach, but Michael Maguire was only in his second season at the club after bringing them premiership glory in his first year. The players have to be held accountable for this unsightly collapse.

Where to from here: Adam Reynolds has retired, Payne Haas is off to the Rabbitohs, and the talk is that the players are not happy with coach Maguire. Mitch Barnett is coming to replace Haas, Dane Gagai to shore up the backline, and Jonah Pezet to reset the halves. They have the entire offseason to sort themselves out, a similar season in 2027 would be completely intolerable for the proud club.

Canberra Raiders
Last year's ladder finish: 1st

Predicted 2026 finish: 7th

Actual finish: 11th

Grade: D

The Raiders took out the minor premiership last season, but the way they crashed out of the finals was not encouraging when it came to predicting their 2026 run. They still should have played finals football this year and, as they showed against the Cowboys in the final round, they still have all the weapons to challenge the top sides. Hudson Young's injury certainly didn't help as they battled for a spot in the Top 8, nor did their ability to lose games they had seemingly already won.

Where to from here: They have lost several players ahead of next season, without making any moves on the player market. They will rely on the juniors coming through as well as halfback Coby Black, who lived up to all the hype during his debut performance against the Cowboys in the final round.

Canterbury Bankstown Bulldogs
Last year's ladder finish: 3rd

Predicted 2026 finish: 2nd

Actual finish: 12th

Grade: F

The Bulldogs receive an F for their 2026 season, simply because they were expected to build on their 2025 success, not crumble in the opposite direction. Lachlan Galvin proved that he is a star of the near future and probably the club's best player through the year, but he played halfback when the team needed a genuine halfback. Moving Matt Burton to centre saw him improve with new found freedom out wide, but moving Stephen Crichton to five-eighth hamstrung his best assets. The whole team continued to look completely lost in attack and only finished as high as they did through defensive resolve, which also faded at the back end of the season. Such a disappointing effort.

Where to from here: Freddy Lussick arrives to hopefully fix one part of the spine. Either Mitchell Woods or Alex Conti should be ready to pull on the No. 7 jersey, Galvin will rise to star status wider of the ruck in the No. 6 jersey, and Burton and Crichton can form the most expensive and lethal of centre combinations. All the club needs then is an attack coach, a dangerous fullback, a new lock and some more grunt in the front row. Easy!

Cronulla Sharks
Last year's ladder finish: 5th

Predicted 2026 finish: 10th

Actual finish: 5th

Grade: TBD

Where to from here: TBD

Dolphins
Last year's ladder finish: 9th

Predicted 2026 finish: 6th

Actual finish: 3rd

Grade: TBD

Where to from here: TBD

Gold Coast Titans
Last year's ladder finish: 16th

Predicted 2026 finish: 14th

Actual finish: 16th

Grade: D

We predicted the Titans would improve slightly under coach Josh Hannay, but they stayed in exactly the same spot. It must be so frustrating for everyone involved to watch the patches of sensational football this club is capable of playing at times. Jayden Campbell remains an elite attacking weapon, Keano Kini an amazing young talent at fullback, Cooper Bai an explosive forward and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui a stoic leader. But, they just lack a couple of key pieces and the drive to play a full 80 minutes of totally committed football.

Where to from here: Apart from welcoming Sharks centre Mawene Hiroti in 2027 they haven't made too many moves on the player market and will be looking instead to improve their systems and fitness. Hannay has a long road ahead of him, with the Bears joining the fray next season, the Titans will face another rung on that ladder they failed to climb at all in 2026.

Manly Sea Eagles
Last year's ladder finish: 10th

Predicted 2026 finish: 13th

Actual finish: 9th

Grade: C

The Sea Eagles started the season where they left off in 2025, losing and looking like a team headed down the ladder. They sacked Anthony Seibold and hired club legend Kieran Foran as head coach and went on an incredible run, which looked certain to take them into the finals. They lost Tom Trbojevic to injury and managed to keep going, but subsequently losing Luke Brooks brought the winning run to a grinding halt. Overall it was a very mixed year, which ended in a frustrating ninth place finish.

Where to from here: They lose Reuben Garrick to the Roosters next year and have made some minor acquisitions. Foran will have a full offseason with the side and they have some promising talent coming through at the club including halfback Joey Walsh. It will be interesting to see whether Foran can recapture the magic of his early days in the job, as they battle again to play finals football.

Melbourne Storm
Last year's ladder finish: 2nd (Runners-up)

Predicted 2026 finish: 8th

Actual finish: 10th

Grade: D

We tipped the Storm to take a slide down the ladder after losing last year's grand final to the Broncos, but no one ever really expects them to miss the finals. They did have a horror year with injuries, with their superstar spine seldom complete for any number of consecutive games. When they did have Harry Grant, Jahrome Hughes and Cameron Munster they were capable of beating anyone, but the bit-part players were unable to lift in their absence. Injuries aside, the Storm didn't look like the Storm at times, with defensive lapses and handling errors driving coach Craig Bellamy up the wall.

Where to from here: Bellamy is going around again as coach, which is handy as it would have been an injustice for him to leave the Storm after that season. They are revamping their backline with the addition of Dolphins flyer Jamayne Isaako and Bulldogs centre Bronson Xerri, while adding Eels forward Kelma Tuilagi. They are also losing a raft of players including Tyran Wishart and Nick Meaney, both to the Bears.

Newcastle Knights
Last year's ladder finish: 17th

Predicted 2026 finish: 13th

Actual finish: 7th

Grade: TBD

Where to from here: TBD

New Zealand Warriors
Last year's ladder finish: 6th

Predicted 2025 finish: 9th

Actual finish: 2nd

Grade: TBD

Where to from here: TBD

North Queensland Cowboys
Last year's ladder finish: 12th

Predicted 2026 finish: 16th

Actual finish: 8th

Grade: C

The fact that the Cowboys somehow snuck into the finals was enough for them to receive a C for their efforts this year. Wildly inconsistent, they could switch on the magic and just about beat anyone, but their defence was appalling at times and ultimately costly. They entered their elimination final needing to tighten up their defence and cut back on their errors, but fell down in both areas. Fullback Scott Drinkwater had a night to both forget and savor in the elimination final against the Sharks, setting up several Cowboys tries while looking completely lost under the high ball.

Overall they got to play in one more game than nine other teams, without ever seriously looking likely to threaten for the title. Their home fans might well remember the season for it's ultimate lowlight: the Round 22 loss to the Roosters which finished in a club record 82-12 flogging.

Where to from here: Scott Drinkwater departs for the Dragons, as the Cowboys go through a minor clean-out. They welcome Joe Chan (Storm), Sione Katoa and Jesse Ramien (both Sharks). Coach Todd Payten will need to spend the entire offseason working on defensive schemes and instilling some commitment to the cause.

Parramatta Eels
Last year's ladder finish: 11th

Predicted 2026 finish: 12th

Actual finish: 13th

Grade: D

The Eels had a frustrating season, often competitive, but rarely consistent. When they were bad, they were very bad, conceding 52 points to the Storm in the opening round, before conceding another 52 to the Titans just five weeks later. They weren't helped by injuries to Mitchell Moses and one-year halves partner Jonah Pezet, but were more often let down by a lack of defensive resolve. Beating the Sharks in Round 26, only to lose to the Dragons in the final round, just about summed up 2026 for the Eels and their long-suffering fans.

Where to from here: They lose a bundle of players for next year, while acquiring Jarome Luai from the Tigers and Jaydn Su'A from the Dragons. It is hard to make any sense of the one-year deal for Luai, even more so with the late-season form of Ronald Volkman, but maybe he will click with Moses and provide more value to the Eels than he did for the Tigers. It is certainly going to be an interesting season for the Eels.

Penrith Panthers
Last year's ladder finish: 7th

Predicted 2026 finish: 1st

Actual finish: 1st

Grade: TBD

Where to from here: TBD

St George Illawarra Dragons
Last year's ladder finish: 15th

Predicted 2026 finish: 17th

Actual finish: 17th

Grade: D

Nailed it. Pre-season favourites for the wooden spoon, the Dragons lived up to all the hype. A mid-season coach sacking didn't help them as much as it did the Sea Eagles, with Dean Young struggling to squeeze any consistency out of the team. We saw flashes of brilliance from Tyrell Sloane, Jacob Liddle and the Dragons' young forward pack, but nothing short of lethargy at times from players like Valentine Holmes, Moses Suli and Clint Gutherson. When in the right mood, they provided some moments of tough opposition, but doing it week-to-week for a full 80 minutes was beyond them.

Where to from here: Nothing but exciting times ahead for the Dragons as they welcome one of the most bountiful player market raids in the history of rugby league. Scott Drinkwater (Cowboys), Keaon Koloamatangi (Rabbitohs), Luke Metcalf (Warriors), Kodi Nikorima (Dolphins), Phillip Sami (Titans) and Connor Watson (Roosters) will all be joining the Dragons' ever-improving young forwards for what should be a complete transformation. Line up now for those 2027 finals tickets, Dragons fans!

South Sydney Rabbitohs
Last year's finish: 14th

Predicted 2025 finish: 5th

Actual finish: 6th

Grade: C

We expected the Rabbitohs to play finals football and considering the injury issues they suffered through the year, they deserve a C for achieving that goal. It was a little ironic then that their season came to an end largely due to yet another injury, this time to Cody Walker. Walker was the spark that fired up Souths' attack all year, without him they were flat and no match for the energetic Knights. Latrell Mitchell's return at the end of the season was definitely a boost; Cameron Murray was his dominating best around the ruck; and Alex Johnston was busy setting try-scoring records on the wing. There were some questions over whether coach Wayne Bennett was best utilising the talents of Jye Gray through the season, with Matthew Dufty disappointing at times at fullback. It was a disappointing end to what was a very promising season.

Where to from here: Payne Haas arrives from the Broncos next season to joining David Fifita in one of the NRL's most intimidating forward packs. They do lose Keaon Koloamatangi from that pack, but Haas is well established as the best forward in the world. The Rabbitohs will squeeze one more season out of Cody Walker, if they can come to an agreement on how much he is worth. Going on their exit from the finals without him, he is just about priceless.

Sydney Roosters
Last year's ladder finish: 8th

Predicted 2025 finish: 4th

Actual finish: 4th

Grade: TBD

Where to from here: TBD

Wests Tigers
Last year's finish: 13th

Predicted 2026 finish: 7th

Actual finish: 15th

Grade: F

What a horribly disappointing season for Tigers fans everywhere. The re-built club, with Jarome Luai at the helm, were expected to break their finals drought and started strongly beating the Cowboys, Warriors, Knights and Raiders in the first eight rounds. And then, Luai announced he was signing with the PNG Chiefs for the club's debut 2028 season. The Tigers imploded and it has been a long road of misery since, conceding 52 to the Sharks, 44 to the Storm, 46 to the Sea Eagles, 68 to the Panthers and 56 to the Raiders along the way. They did upset the Roosters in Round 25 to bring a little joy to the black-and-gold army.

Where to from here: Coach Benji Marshall has to somehow wipe 2026 from the players' minds, as he focusses their attention on returning to finals football in 2027. They have made two very astute acquisitions in Jake Averillo (Dolphins) and Jayden Brailey (Raiders). Both are no-nonsense professionals who will sharpen up the Tigers' play and their attitude.
